pip install redirected to non-PyPI index / find-links (dependency confusion) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts pip invocations that pull packages from an --index-url / --extra-index-url / --find-links pointing anywhere other than pypi.org or files.pythonhosted.org. This is the article's 'custom web server / alternate index' hosting-layer abuse used to serve malicious packages or dependency-confusion payloads. Rationale: Anchors on the article's custom-index hosting layer using the exact pip flags (--index-url/--extra-index-url/--find-links) and excludes the two canonical PyPI hosts (pypi.org, files.pythonhosted.org) the article names as the legitimate download path. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/the-serpents-tongue-luring-the-python-out-of-its-den/ • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/teampcp-supply-chain-attacks/ • https://www.okta.com/blog/threat-intelligence/defending_against_team_pcp_software_supply_chain_attacks/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal corporate PyPI mirror (Artifactory/Nexus/devpi) configured via --index-url on the CLI
  • CI/CD build agents installing from a private package feed URL
  • Developers testing a local devpi/pypiserver during package development
  • Air-gapped hosts using --find-links against an offline wheelhouse directory
Suppression filter
| where not(ProcessCommandLine has_any ("artifactory","nexus","devpi","pkgs.dev.azure.com","codeartifact","jfrog.io"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract the index/find-links host from ProcessCommandLine; is it a known internal mirror or an external/unrecognised domain or raw IP? Check WHOIS/first-seen. 2) Contain: if the host is untrusted, isolate the endpoint, capture the pip cache and any newly created site-packages dirs, and block the domain/IP at the proxy. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host for child process spawns from the installed package, .pth writes into site-packages, and outbound C2 from python; check whether PIP_INDEX_URL/PIP_CONFIG_FILE was set persistently to make the redirect survive.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where (FileName in~ ("pip.exe","pip3.exe") or (FileName in~ ("python.exe","python3.exe","python3","python") and ProcessCommandLine has "pip"))
| where ProcessCommandLine has "install"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--index-url","--extra-index-url","--find-links")
| where not(ProcessCommandLine has_any ("pypi.org","files.pythonhosted.org"))
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\pip.exe","\\pip3.exe","\\python.exe","\\python3.exe")
| where CommandLine has "install"
| where CommandLine has_any ("--index-url","--extra-index-url","--find-links")
| where not(CommandLine has_any ("pypi.org","files.pythonhosted.org"))
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Pip Install From Non-PyPI Index or Find-Links Source
id: 6b2f9c1a-8d4e-4a7b-9f21-3c7e5a1d0f42
description: Detects pip installing packages from an alternate index URL or find-links location that is not the official PyPI, matching the custom-repository hosting abuse described by Cisco Talos.
references:
  - https://blog.talosintelligence.com/the-serpents-tongue-luring-the-python-out-of-its-den/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/14
tags:
  - attack.t1195.002
  - attack.t1059.006
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_img:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\pip.exe'
      - '\pip3.exe'
      - '\python.exe'
      - '\python3.exe'
  selection_flags:
    CommandLine|contains: 'install'
  selection_index:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '--index-url'
      - '--extra-index-url'
      - '--find-links'
  filter_official:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'pypi.org'
      - 'files.pythonhosted.org'
  condition: selection_img and selection_flags and selection_index and not filter_official
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\pip.exe OR *\pip3.exe OR *\python.exe OR *\python3.exe OR *\Python.exe) @CommandLine:*install* (@CommandLine:*--index-url* OR @CommandLine:*--extra-index-url* OR @CommandLine:*--find-links*) -(@CommandLine:*pypi.org* OR @CommandLine:*files.pythonhosted.org*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/(pip3?|python3?)(\.exe)?$/i
| CommandLine=/\binstall\b/i
| CommandLine=/--(index-url|extra-index-url|find-links)/i
| NOT (CommandLine=/(pypi\.org|files\.pythonhosted\.org)/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())

Python setup.py install-time code execution spawning shell/LOLBin AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the article's core sdist build-hook abuse: setup.py executes arbitrary code the moment pip builds/installs a source distribution. Fires when a Python process running setup.py (or its pip parent) spawns a shell, script host, or download LOLBin. Rationale: Uses the article's central claim that setup.py 'executes automatically during installation, allowing for the execution of arbitrary code' — pivoting on the setup.py parent command line spawning a shell/download LOLBin. Falcon variant approximates via python/pip parent because FDR ProcessRollup2 does not expose parent command line. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/the-serpents-tongue-luring-the-python-out-of-its-den/ • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/teampcp-supply-chain-attacks/ • https://www.wiz.io/blog/durabletask-teampcp-supply-chain-attack
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.006 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legit packages with C/C++ extensions whose setup.py shells out to a compiler wrapper or configure script during build
  • setup.py calling git.exe/curl to fetch version metadata or submodules at build time
  • Developer running 'python setup.py test' that invokes a shell-based test harness
  • Vendored build scripts that call certutil/bitsadmin for legitimate artifact retrieval on locked-down build agents
Suppression filter
| where not(ProcessCommandLine has_any ("cl.exe","gcc","clang","cmake","configure","vcvars"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the child command line and the package name/path from InitiatingProcessCommandLine; decode any base64/encoded payload and identify the package being installed. 2) Contain: kill the process tree, isolate the host, and quarantine the sdist tarball + pip cache; pull the package from the resolved index and preserve setup.py. 3) Hunt: check other hosts that installed the same package name/version, look for .pth persistence written into site-packages, credential-file reads, and outbound connections from the python process during the install window.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "setup.py"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","bash","sh","bash.exe","sh.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "setup.py"
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","bash","sh")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Malicious .pth file dropped into site-packages by pip/python AIInstallation Medium
Hunts install-time persistence via a .pth file written into site-packages/dist-packages. Python auto-executes any line in a .pth file beginning with 'import' on every interpreter start, giving transient-to-persistent code execution — the TeamPCP litellm_init.pth technique that aligns with the article's persistent build-hook abuse. Rationale: Grounded in the article's 'Persistent' build-hook abuse row (setup.py+pyproject.toml, sdist+wheel) and corroborated by TeamPCP's litellm_init.pth in-package persistence; the site-packages/dist-packages path plus a .pth extension written by pip/python is the exact drop location, with the two standard tooling .pth files excluded. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/the-serpents-tongue-luring-the-python-out-of-its-den/ • https://www.wiz.io/blog/durabletask-teampcp-supply-chain-attack • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/teampcp-supply-chain-attacks/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1546 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Editable installs (pip install -e .) dropping __editable__.<pkg>.pth or setuptools' generated .pth
  • Packages like matplotlib/pywin32/virtualenv legitimately shipping a .pth to extend sys.path
  • conda/virtualenv creation writing standard path-configuration .pth files
  • IDE (PyCharm/VS Code) creating a project .pth for interpreter path management
Suppression filter
| where not(FileName startswith "__editable__" or FileName in~ ("__editable___finder.pth","virtualenv.pth","pywin32.pth"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the .pth contents — a benign one contains only directory paths; flag any line starting with 'import' or containing exec/eval/base64. 2) Contain: if it executes code, isolate the host, delete/quarantine the .pth, and identify the parent package from the surrounding .dist-info. 3) Hunt: enumerate all interpreters on the host for the same .pth, sweep other endpoints that installed the same package/version, and correlate to any non-PyPI index redirect (UC1) or setup.py execution (UC2) in the same install window.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where FileName endswith ".pth"
| where FolderPath has_any ("site-packages","dist-packages")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("pip.exe","pip3.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","python3")
| where not(FileName in~ ("easy-install.pth","distutils-precedence.pth"))
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where TargetFileName endswith ".pth"
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("site-packages","dist-packages")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("pip.exe","pip3.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","python3")
| where not(TargetFileName in~ ("easy-install.pth","distutils-precedence.pth"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Persistent PIP_ index/config environment variable set in registry AIInstallation High
Alerts when a PIP_INDEX_URL / PIP_EXTRA_INDEX_URL / PIP_FIND_LINKS / PIP_CONFIG_FILE environment variable is written to the user or system Environment registry key. Per the article, any pip CLI arg converts to a PIP_<UPPER_LONG_NAME> env var — persisting one silently redirects ALL future pip installs to attacker infrastructure. Rationale: Directly operationalises the article's statement that any pip argument becomes a PIP_<UPPER_LONG_NAME> env var (naming PIP_CONFIG_FILE and PIP_FIND_LINKS) — writing these under the Environment registry key is a low-FP, high-fidelity redirect/persistence primitive. Falcon left empty: FDR does not reliably ship Session Manager\Environment writes as an AsepValueUpdate event. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/the-serpents-tongue-luring-the-python-out-of-its-den/ • https://www.okta.com/blog/threat-intelligence/defending_against_team_pcp_software_supply_chain_attacks/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1112 T1574.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer permanently pointing pip at a corporate mirror by setting PIP_INDEX_URL in user environment
  • IT provisioning script/GPO that pushes PIP_CONFIG_FILE to a managed pip.ini for all developers
  • CI runner bootstrap that exports PIP_EXTRA_INDEX_URL for a private feed
  • DevOps setting PIP_TARGET/PIP_PREFIX for a shared build environment
Suppression filter
| where not(RegistryValueData has_any ("artifactory","nexus","devpi","pkgs.dev.azure.com","codeartifact","jfrog.io"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: read RegistryValueData — is the URL/config path an approved internal mirror or an external/unknown host? Identify the writing process (InitiatingProcessCommandLine) and whether it was interactive or scripted. 2) Contain: if untrusted, delete the value, block the destination at the proxy, and audit any pip installs that ran after the value was set. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC1 (non-PyPI index installs) and UC2/UC3 on the same host and any host sharing the GPO/provisioning source; verify no pip.ini/pip.conf on disk was also modified to the same destination.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType == "RegistryValueSet"
| where RegistryKey has_any (@"\Environment", @"Session Manager\Environment")
| where RegistryValueName in~ ("PIP_INDEX_URL","PIP_EXTRA_INDEX_URL","PIP_FIND_LINKS","PIP_CONFIG_FILE","PIP_TARGET","PIP_PREFIX")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventType == "RegistryValueSet"
| where RegistryKey has_any (@"\Environment", @"Session Manager\Environment")
| where RegistryValue in~ ("PIP_INDEX_URL","PIP_EXTRA_INDEX_URL","PIP_FIND_LINKS","PIP_CONFIG_FILE","PIP_TARGET","PIP_PREFIX")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:

author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation

detection:

            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'

Miasma/AsyncAPI first-stage: node spawns detached 'node -e' downloader referencing IPFS/sync.js AIDelivery High
Hunts the AsyncAPI supply-chain first stage: a Node process spawns a detached child `node -e '<obfuscated>'` whose inline string table carries the plaintext IPFS gateway URL, the stage-2 CID, and the drop filename sync.js. Fires on package-import-triggered download rather than any npm lifecycle hook. Rationale: Anchored on verbatim strings from the shipped downloader string table (both IPFS CIDs, the ipfs.io gateway path, drop name sync.js) combined with the node->node -e detached-spawn shape. CIDs and the download-to-per-user-dir behaviour are confirmed by Wiz and SafeDep, so a require()-triggered node -e hit on these is unambiguous. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/m-red-team-asyncapi-supply-chain-compromise-via-github-actions • https://safedep.io/asyncapi-generator-supply-chain-attack-miasma-rat/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/miasma-malware-targets-npm-packages-and.html
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer legitimately scripting an IPFS pin/fetch with `node -e` against ipfs.io during dApp/Web3 work
  • CI job that inlines a node -e helper referencing a file literally named sync.js (rare)
  • Security researcher detonating the sample in a sandbox that is also EDR-monitored
  • Internal reproduction/IR testing of this exact payload after the advisory
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full child ProcessCommandLine and confirm it contains an ipfs.io CID and sync.js; check the parent node process's working dir / project for an installed @asyncapi/specs@6.11.2(-alpha.1), @asyncapi/generator@3.3.1, generator-helpers@1.1.1 or generator-components@0.7.1. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the detached node child, and quarantine %LOCALAPPDATA%\NodeJS\sync.js (or ~/Library/Application Support/NodeJS, ~/.local/share/NodeJS). 3) Hunt: pivot on the host for outbound to 85.137.53.71 and for ~/.config/.miasma/ artifacts and miasma-monitor persistence; rotate any npm/GitHub/AWS tokens and SSH keys exposed on that host.

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc

Miasma stage-2 dropped: sync.js written to per-user NodeJS data directory AIInstallation High
Detects the second-stage loader landing on disk. The downloader writes the encrypted IPFS object as sync.js into the per-user Node data dir (%LOCALAPPDATA%\NodeJS on Windows, ~/Library/Application Support/NodeJS on macOS, ~/.local/share/NodeJS on Linux), written by a node process. Rationale: The drop filename (sync.js) and the exact per-user NodeJS data directories are stated verbatim in the article and corroborated by SafeDep/Wiz as the stage-2 write location. A node-written sync.js in that dir has effectively no benign meaning — Node itself never creates that file there. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/m-red-team-asyncapi-supply-chain-compromise-via-github-actions • https://safedep.io/asyncapi-generator-supply-chain-attack-miasma-rat/

Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Unrelated Node tooling that coincidentally creates a cache file named sync.js under an app dir containing the token 'NodeJS' (uncommon)
  • EDR replay/rehydration of a quarantined sample regenerating the file
  • IR/forensic copy of the artifact onto a monitored analyst workstation
  • Backup/sync agent restoring an infected user profile
Response runbook
1) Triage: hash the dropped sync.js and compare against known stage-2 loaders (~8.24-8.25 MB); confirm the writing process is node and identify the parent project with an affected @asyncapi package. 2) Contain: quarantine the file, kill any node process executing it, and isolate the host. 3) Hunt: check for outbound to 85.137.53.71, for ~/.config/.miasma/ identity/lock files and miasma-monitor persistence, and enumerate other hosts that installed the same @asyncapi versions in the compromise window.

Miasma stage-2 executed: node runs sync.js from NodeJS data directory AIInstallation High
Detects execution of the dropped loader — a node process launched with a command line pointing at sync.js inside the per-user NodeJS data directory. This is the detached persistence/loader run that decrypts and evaluates the M-RED-TEAM stage-3 implant. Rationale: Distinct pivot from the first stage: instead of an inline node -e, this catches node executing the on-disk sync.js by path (NodeJS dir + sync.js), the stage-2 loader run. Path and filename are article-verbatim and corroborated as the loader location. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/m-red-team-asyncapi-supply-chain-compromise-via-github-actions • https://safedep.io/asyncapi-generator-supply-chain-attack-miasma-rat/

1) Triage: capture full ProcessCommandLine and the sync.js path/hash; confirm the parent is a detached node (unref'd) and not an interactive dev session. 2) Contain: kill the process tree, isolate the host, quarantine sync.js. 3) Hunt: look for the resulting HTTP C2 to 85.137.53.71 (three ports), for miasma-monitor persistence and ~/.config/.miasma/ paths, and sweep the fleet for the same loader path; force credential rotation on the affected account.

Miasma M-RED-TEAM HTTP C2 beacon to 85.137.53.71 AICommand & Control Medium
Detects any host contacting the confirmed Miasma/M-RED-TEAM HTTP C2 endpoint 85.137.53.71 (operated on three ports). This is the stage-3 implant's primary command-and-control channel and a hard network IOC. Rationale: 85.137.53.71 is a dedicated Miasma HTTP C2 host independently confirmed by Wiz, SafeDep, and The Hacker News (three ports). A hard-IOC network match with near-zero benign traffic; projecting the initiating process/port surfaces the beaconing binary and channel for triage. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/m-red-team-asyncapi-supply-chain-compromise-via-github-actions • https://safedep.io/asyncapi-generator-supply-chain-attack-miasma-rat/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/miasma-malware-targets-npm-packages-and.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel/scanning appliance or a SOC honeypot deliberately probing the C2 IP
  • Sandbox detonation egressing to the live C2
  • Researcher curl/browser test against the IP from a corporate host
  • Shared-egress NAT causing a benign-looking source if the true infected host isn't attributed
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process (expect node) and the destination port; confirm the host installed an affected @asyncapi version and has %LOCALAPPDATA%\NodeJS\sync.js. 2) Contain: block 85.137.53.71 at the egress/firewall, isolate the host, and terminate the beaconing node process. 3) Hunt: correlate to the sync.js drop/exec and the node -e downloader on the same host, sweep all egress logs for other hosts hitting the IP, and rotate npm/GitHub/AWS/SSH credentials that were reachable from the compromised host.

| where DstIpAddr == "85.137.53.71"

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)

// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["f873941d1907a97dc6c718fdecf59fd7d91f3f8212da2f7e5314b878b88bdc0b", "9e214f38537e69bf51c7fa1ddd35ae495e9cb897231ec010baf9e4f29407ee9a", "bfaeb987faa6de2b5a5eb63b1233d055215b09b0349a9394f2175fd7cdf385e4", "34014776d3d3ff11bc4439b02fd7ac0f02a887eb3a052eeaffd236e2f6db8ad1", "082d733db0687dcd768104972b065d4b58cb1e6043688c6c20fa3702337f36ab", "9b2e65db653ca8575c9b10eefb9a80c6006404812c2ec212bf5675e3c690233b", "22bf76fe317ea6769bd38619bd440e42d119bd6b", "a7e18d96efd3cdb127ef4cdcad9e3ad26c482bf2", "9890950adcbc2478e7a080234f053214adbad44e", "c70e105e212ff3c1daa04bb2a62507717f296b0b", "c8cb3f6d5b90c46686d2bf531dc1a5786e27edc5"]);
union

        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,

| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Likely
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Exposure to revoked vulnerable UEFI shims (CVE-2026-8863 / CVE-2026-10797)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Vulnerable UEFI shim/GRUB bootloader written to the EFI System Partition · [LLM] EFI System Partition mounted via mountvol /S (rogue shim staging) · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Exposure to revoked vulnerable UEFI shims (CVE-2026-8863 / CVE-2026-10797) AIExploitation Medium
Surfaces managed endpoints that Defender TVM flags as carrying the ESET-reported vulnerable UEFI shim bootloaders (versions <=0.9) covered by CVE-2026-8863 and CVE-2026-10797. These devices remain exploitable for Secure Boot bypass until Microsoft's June 9 2026 dbx revocation (KB5101650) is applied, so this is a posture hunt to prioritise dbx rollout. Rationale: Pivots on the two CVE IDs assigned by CERT/CC (VU#616257) and ESET to the reported shims; TVM CVE mapping is high-fidelity for prioritising which hosts still need the June 2026 dbx update. No FP concept — it is a vulnerability-inventory lookup. Cross-checked against: • https://kb.cert.org/vuls/id/616257 • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/11-old-microsoft-signed-linux-uefi.html • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/14/eset-uefi-secure-boot-bypass/
ATT&CKT1542 T1542.003
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • TVM CVE-to-firmware mapping lag means recently-patched (dbx applied) hosts may still show as vulnerable for one scan cycle
  • Linux/dual-boot hosts legitimately shipping shim as part of the distro but already on shim >=15.7
  • Devices where the third-party UEFI CA is disabled in firmware are not actually exploitable but may still list the shim software
  • Air-gapped or offline devices whose TVM data is stale
Suppression filter
| where isnotempty(RecommendedSecurityUpdate)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the device trusts the Microsoft Corporation UEFI CA 2011 third-party cert and whether the June 9 2026 dbx update (KB5101650) is installed. 2) Contain: schedule/push the dbx revocation update; where BitLocker is present, validate recovery keys are escrowed before the dbx change to avoid boot lockout. 3) Hunt: on any exposed host, pivot to UC-2/UC-3 to check whether a rogue shim was actually written to the ESP or the partition was mounted, and review boot integrity / measured-boot logs.

Vulnerable UEFI shim/GRUB bootloader written to the EFI System Partition AIInstallation Medium
Detects a shim or GRUB2 EFI bootloader binary (shimx64.efi, grubx64.efi, mmx64.efi, bootx64.efi and 32-bit variants) being created or modified under an \EFI\ path — the 'bring your own vulnerable shim' technique ESET describes, where an attacker drops a Microsoft-signed but pre-revocation shim onto any UEFI system to bypass Secure Boot. Highest signal on Windows-only endpoints that should never have Linux shim/GRUB binaries on the ESP. Rationale: Uses the exact shim/GRUB EFI filenames from the shim ecosystem the article names (shim + second-stage GRUB2) constrained to the \EFI\ system-partition path. On a Windows-managed fleet, a Linux shim/GRUB binary appearing on the ESP is a strong 'attacker staged a pre-revocation shim' signal rather than any Microsoft boot component (bootmgfw.efi). Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/forgotten-uefi-shims-undermining-secure-boot/ • https://kb.cert.org/vuls/id/616257
ATT&CKT1542.003 T1542
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Linux install or dual-boot setup writing shim/GRUB to the ESP
  • OEM/firmware recovery or imaging tooling refreshing fallback \EFI\Boot\bootx64.efi
  • Endpoint backup/restore software that snapshots and rewrites the ESP
  • Legitimate shim upgrade (>=15.7) pushed by a Linux distro package manager on genuinely dual-boot hosts
  • Enterprise Linux deployment/MDT task sequences staging boot files
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("grub-install","bootmgr.exe","setup.exe","dism.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Windows\SoftwareDistribution\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify InitiatingProcess writing the file — legitimate installers (setup.exe, grub-install, firmware updaters) vs. an interactive shell/LOLBin; compute and compare the file's Authenticode hash against the 11 dbx-revoked hashes from the ESET advisory. 2) Contain: if the writer is untrusted or the hash matches a revoked shim, isolate the host, preserve the ESP contents, and force the dbx (KB5101650) update to neutralise the shim. 3) Hunt: check UC-3 for a preceding mountvol /S on the same host, review boot configuration (bcdedit) changes, and look for known bootkit artefacts (Bootkitty, HybridPetya, BlackLotus).
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where FileName in~ ("shimx64.efi","shimia32.efi","grubx64.efi","grubia32.efi","mmx64.efi","mmia32.efi","bootx64.efi","bootia32.efi")
| where FolderPath has @"\EFI\"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("shimx64.efi","shimia32.efi","grubx64.efi","grubia32.efi","mmx64.efi","mmia32.efi","bootx64.efi","bootia32.efi")
| where TargetFilePath has @"\EFI\"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

EFI System Partition mounted via mountvol /S (rogue shim staging) AIInstallation Medium
Detects execution of mountvol.exe with the /S switch, which mounts the normally-hidden EFI System Partition to a drive letter — the prerequisite step an attacker uses on Windows to drop a pre-revocation shim onto the ESP before deploying a bootkit. This LOLBin flag is extremely rare in normal operations, making it a high-signal hunting pivot. Rationale: mountvol /S is the documented, rarely-used command to expose the EFI System Partition on UEFI systems; pairing it with the shim-write in UC-2 reconstructs the on-host staging chain for ESET's bring-your-own-shim bypass. Command flag is concrete and article-adjacent (ESP manipulation), not a generic template. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/forgotten-uefi-shims-undermining-secure-boot/ • https://kb.cert.org/vuls/id/616257
ATT&CKT1542 T1542.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmin troubleshooting boot/BCD issues or manually inspecting the ESP
  • OEM firmware/BIOS update utilities that mount the ESP to stage capsule updates
  • Backup/imaging software mounting the ESP for full-disk capture
  • Windows servicing or driver-signing workflows that touch the ESP
  • IT scripts that mount the ESP to repair bootmgfw.efi after a failed update
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Windows\System32\" or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the parent process and user launching mountvol /S — a scripted/interactive shell (cmd, powershell, unknown binary) is far more suspicious than a signed OEM updater; note any drive letter assigned. 2) Contain: if launched outside an approved change window or by an untrusted parent, isolate the host and inspect the newly-mounted ESP for shim/GRUB binaries (feed into UC-2) before dismounting. 3) Hunt: correlate on the same host and 10-minute window for .efi writes to \EFI\, bcdedit boot-order changes, and any of the 11 revoked shim hashes; verify dbx (KB5101650) status.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "mountvol.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/s"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\mountvol.exe"
| where CommandLine has "/s"
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Kimai authenticated session activity with no preceding form-login POST (forged remember-me cookie) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts Kimai (Symfony) authenticated access to admin/API/user routes from a source IP that never submitted a POST to the login form in the lookback window. CVE-2026-52824 lets an attacker with the publicly-known default APP_SECRET forge the KIMAI_REMEMBER cookie and be silently auto-authenticated, so the account 'logs in' without any credential submission crossing the wire. Rationale: Uses Kimai's KIMAI_REMEMBER remember-me cookie name and Symfony's form-login POST as the two anchors from the article; the anti-join (authenticated route access from an IP that never POSTed to login) is the observable footprint of a forged remember-me cookie since Symfony auto-authenticates without a credential exchange. Cross-checked GitLab advisory and Symfony login docs. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/kimai/kimai/CVE-2026-52824/ • https://symfony.com/doc/current/security/login_link.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1550.004
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate 'remember me' users whose original POST /login happened before the lookback window began
  • SSO / reverse-proxy that terminates auth upstream and forwards without a Kimai form POST
  • Corporate NAT egress where one IP both logs in and is reused by an automation account
  • Health-check / monitoring probes hitting /api with a stored service session
  • Load balancer or CDN rewriting the client source IP so the login POST and the app request appear on different IPs
Suppression filter
| where UserAgent !has "HealthCheck" and UserAgent !has "kube-probe" and CIp !in (dynamic(["<corporate-egress-not-needed:leave-empty-or-populate-org-CIDRs-in-loginIPs-let>"]))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the CIp's full request timeline; confirm the first authenticated request truly has no prior POST to /login and inspect whether Cookie carried KIMAI_REMEMBER but never a fresh PHPSESSID handshake. Identify which Kimai account (CsUsername) the session maps to and whether it is super_admin. 2) Contain: rotate APP_SECRET immediately (invalidates all forged cookies/links), force-logout all sessions, and require password reset + enable 2FA on privileged accounts. 3) Hunt: check whether the same IP/UA hit login-link URLs (hash/expires/user params) or created users, changed rates, or exported timesheets; confirm the instance was on Kimai < 2.58.0 with the default secret.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let loginIPs = AppServiceHTTPLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where CsMethod == "POST" and CsUriStem has "login"   // Kimai/Symfony form-login check route
    | distinct CIp;
AppServiceHTTPLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where CsUriStem has_any ("/admin/", "/api/", "/user")   // authenticated Kimai surfaces
| where ScStatus >= 200 and ScStatus < 400
| where CsUsername != "" or Cookie has "KIMAI_REMEMBER"    // session was authenticated
| where CIp !in (loginIPs)                                 // but no form login ever seen from this IP
| summarize FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Requests = count(), Paths = make_set(CsUriStem, 20) by CIp, UserAgent, CsUsername
| order by FirstSeen desc

Kimai forged Symfony login-link request (user+expires+hash signed URL) to super_admin AIExploitation Medium
Hunts inbound GET requests whose query string carries the Symfony passwordless login-link signature triad — user, expires and hash. With the default APP_SECRET (CVE-2026-52824) an unauthenticated attacker can mint valid login links for any account, so a burst of these signed URLs (especially targeting the id=1/super_admin identifier) from external IPs is a direct forgery indicator. Rationale: Grounded in the article's explicit 'LoginLink signatures' forgery vector and the Symfony-documented login-link parameter triad (user/expires/hash); matching all three tokens in the query string is a distinctive single-event signature that fires even without knowing Kimai's exact check-route path. Cross-checked Symfony login-link docs and the GitLab advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/kimai/kimai/CVE-2026-52824/ • https://symfony.com/doc/current/security/login_link.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1078.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Organisation legitimately uses Symfony/Kimai passwordless login links for real users
  • Password-reset or email-verification links that reuse a similar signed-URL shape
  • Security scanners (Burp/ZAP) fuzzing query parameters named user/expires/hash
  • Uptime monitors replaying a captured login-link URL
  • Other Symfony apps behind the same proxy emitting UriSigner-style links
Suppression filter
| where CsUriStem !has "password-reset" and UserAgent !has_any ("ZAP", "Burp", "Nuclei", "masscan")
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract TargetUser from CsUriQuery; determine whether the value corresponds to the id=1/super_admin username and whether the request returned 200/302 (link accepted). Check the source IP's geo/ASN and whether it is external. 2) Contain: if the login link was accepted, rotate APP_SECRET (invalidates every forged link), kill active sessions, reset the targeted account's password and enforce 2FA. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same CIp/UA for subsequent authenticated admin/API activity and for KIMAI_REMEMBER-cookie sessions; verify the deployment ran the default APP_SECRET on Kimai < 2.58.0.
AppServiceHTTPLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where CsMethod == "GET"
| where CsUriQuery has "hash=" and CsUriQuery has "expires=" and CsUriQuery has "user="   // Symfony login-link signed URL triad
| extend TargetUser = extract(@"(?i)user=([^&]+)", 1, CsUriQuery)
| project TimeGenerated, CIp, UserAgent, CsUriStem, CsUriQuery, TargetUser, ScStatus, CsUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Shai-Hulud npm worm payload/workflow file drop (bundle.js, setup_bun.js, shai-hulud-workflow.yml) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the Shai-Hulud supply-chain worm dropping its self-replicating payload and CI persistence file onto developer machines during npm install. Fires on the confirmed malicious bundle.js SHA256 or the distinctive worm filenames written by node/npm. Rationale: Uses the second-source-confirmed Shai-Hulud bundle.js SHA256 (46faab8a...) and the campaign's distinctive filenames (shai-hulud-workflow.yml, setup_bun.js, bun_environment.js) named across Unit42/Wiz/Datadog write-ups of the article's flagship campaign; hash+filename anchors make this near-zero-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/npm-supply-chain-attack/ • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/ • https://www.wiz.io/blog/shai-hulud-npm-supply-chain-attack
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer legitimately named a file bundle.js under a non-malicious .github/workflows path (rare — that dir holds YAML, not JS)
  • Security researcher intentionally detonating a Shai-Hulud sample in a sandbox/analysis VM
  • EDR/AV quarantine copies of the payload re-triggering the file-write event from the quarantine folder
  • Threat-intel/IR team staging IOC files named setup_bun.js for tabletop or purple-team exercises
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Windows Defender\", @"\Quarantine\") or DeviceName has_any ("sandbox","malware-lab"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the writing process (InitiatingProcessFileName node.exe/npm) and the folder — a real hit is bundle.js/setup_bun.js executed during an npm/bun install in a repo working dir. Check the file SHA256 against 46faab8a... 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, revoke and rotate all npm tokens, GitHub PATs, and cloud (AWS/GCP/Azure) keys used from it; check GitHub for a newly-created public repo named 'Shai-Hulud' and any 'shai-hulud-workflow.yml' pushed to your repos. 3) HUNT: Pivot to outbound connections to webhook.site from the same host, enumerate every package version installed in the last 24h, and scope other developers who installed the same dependency.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (SHA256 == "46faab8ab153fae6e80e7cca38eab363075bb524edd79e42269217a083628f09")
     or FileName in~ ("shai-hulud-workflow.yml","setup_bun.js","bun_environment.js")
     or (FileName =~ "bundle.js" and FolderPath has @"\.github\workflows")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (TargetFileSHA256 == "46faab8ab153fae6e80e7cca38eab363075bb524edd79e42269217a083628f09")
     or TargetFileName in~ ("shai-hulud-workflow.yml","setup_bun.js","bun_environment.js")
     or (TargetFileName =~ "bundle.js" and TargetFilePath has @"\.github\workflows")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath,
          TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Shai-Hulud credential exfiltration: node/npm outbound to webhook.site AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the Shai-Hulud worm's credential exfiltration stage where the postinstall payload beacons harvested npm/GitHub/cloud tokens to the hardcoded webhook.site drop (bb8ca5f6-4175-45d2-b042-fc9ebb8170b7). Pairs the webhook.site destination with a node/npm/bun/git initiating process to cut the FP from legit webhook testing. Rationale: Anchors on the second-source-confirmed hardcoded exfil host webhook.site (Shai-Hulud endpoint bb8ca5f6-4175-45d2-b042-fc9ebb8170b7) but requires a node/npm/bun/git initiating process so it fires on postinstall exfil, not a developer manually testing a webhook in a browser. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/npm-supply-chain-attack/ • https://www.wiz.io/blog/shai-hulud-npm-supply-chain-attack • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/
ATT&CKT1567 T1552.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer legitimately using webhook.site to test an outbound webhook from a Node app during development
  • CI runner (node/git) hitting a webhook.site URL configured in a test suite or integration fixture
  • QA automation posting to webhook.site as a capture endpoint
  • Internal tooling that uses webhook.site free-tier bins for prototyping event delivery
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("install","postinstall","ci","exec") and not (DeviceName has_any ("build-agent","ci-runner") and InitiatingProcessAccountName has "jenkins")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the full RemoteUrl/DNS path — a real hit posts to a webhook.site UUID bin (campaign default bb8ca5f6-4175-45d2-b042-fc9ebb8170b7) shortly after an npm/bun install; check InitiatingProcessCommandLine for a package install and correlate with a bundle.js/setup_bun.js write in the last hour. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, immediately rotate npm tokens, GitHub PATs, and AWS/GCP/Azure keys from that machine, and block webhook.site at egress. 3) HUNT: Search GitHub audit for a new public 'Shai-Hulud' repo or 'shai-hulud-workflow.yml' commits under affected users, and scope every other host that installed the same package version.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "webhook.site"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","bun.exe","git.exe","curl.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has "webhook.site"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Shai-Hulud Credential Exfiltration to webhook.site via node/npm
id: 2b9e4d17-5c60-49af-8f31-a0d6c2e51f4a
description: Detects Node/npm/bun/git process resolving or connecting to webhook.site, the Shai-Hulud worm's hardcoded token exfiltration endpoint

  - https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/npm-supply-chain-attack/

      - '\bun.exe'

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS where (DNS.query="webhook.site" OR DNS.query="*.webhook.site") by DNS.src DNS.dest DNS.query | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command Exploitation High
Encoded or obfuscated PowerShell — common across loaders, recon, and post-exploitation.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.execution
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'
            - '-ExecutionPolicy Bypass'
    condition: selection_image and selection_args
falsepositives:
    - DevOps tooling that legitimately uses encoded command for
      cross-shell escaping
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("46faab8ab153fae6e80e7cca38eab363075bb524edd79e42269217a083628f09", "62ee164b9b306250c1172583f138c9614139264f889fa99614903c12755468d0", "f099c5d9ec417d4445a0328ac0ada9cde79fc37410914103ae9c609cbc0ee068", "cbb9bc5a8496243e02f3cc080efbe3e4a1430ba0671f2e43a202bf45b05479cd", "a3894003ad1d293ba96d77881ccd2071446dc3f65f434669b49b3da92421901a") or SHA1 in~ ("46faab8ab153fae6e80e7cca38eab363075bb524edd79e42269217a083628f09", "62ee164b9b306250c1172583f138c9614139264f889fa99614903c12755468d0", "f099c5d9ec417d4445a0328ac0ada9cde79fc37410914103ae9c609cbc0ee068", "cbb9bc5a8496243e02f3cc080efbe3e4a1430ba0671f2e43a202bf45b05479cd", "a3894003ad1d293ba96d77881ccd2071446dc3f65f434669b49b3da92421901a") or MD5 in~ ("46faab8ab153fae6e80e7cca38eab363075bb524edd79e42269217a083628f09", "62ee164b9b306250c1172583f138c9614139264f889fa99614903c12755468d0", "f099c5d9ec417d4445a0328ac0ada9cde79fc37410914103ae9c609cbc0ee068", "cbb9bc5a8496243e02f3cc080efbe3e4a1430ba0671f2e43a202bf45b05479cd", "a3894003ad1d293ba96d77881ccd2071446dc3f65f434669b49b3da92421901a")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("46faab8ab153fae6e80e7cca38eab363075bb524edd79e42269217a083628f09", "62ee164b9b306250c1172583f138c9614139264f889fa99614903c12755468d0", "f099c5d9ec417d4445a0328ac0ada9cde79fc37410914103ae9c609cbc0ee068", "cbb9bc5a8496243e02f3cc080efbe3e4a1430ba0671f2e43a202bf45b05479cd", "a3894003ad1d293ba96d77881ccd2071446dc3f65f434669b49b3da92421901a") or SHA1 in~ ("46faab8ab153fae6e80e7cca38eab363075bb524edd79e42269217a083628f09", "62ee164b9b306250c1172583f138c9614139264f889fa99614903c12755468d0", "f099c5d9ec417d4445a0328ac0ada9cde79fc37410914103ae9c609cbc0ee068", "cbb9bc5a8496243e02f3cc080efbe3e4a1430ba0671f2e43a202bf45b05479cd", "a3894003ad1d293ba96d77881ccd2071446dc3f65f434669b49b3da92421901a") or MD5 in~ ("46faab8ab153fae6e80e7cca38eab363075bb524edd79e42269217a083628f09", "62ee164b9b306250c1172583f138c9614139264f889fa99614903c12755468d0", "f099c5d9ec417d4445a0328ac0ada9cde79fc37410914103ae9c609cbc0ee068", "cbb9bc5a8496243e02f3cc080efbe3e4a1430ba0671f2e43a202bf45b05479cd", "a3894003ad1d293ba96d77881ccd2071446dc3f65f434669b49b3da92421901a")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["46faab8ab153fae6e80e7cca38eab363075bb524edd79e42269217a083628f09", "62ee164b9b306250c1172583f138c9614139264f889fa99614903c12755468d0", "f099c5d9ec417d4445a0328ac0ada9cde79fc37410914103ae9c609cbc0ee068", "cbb9bc5a8496243e02f3cc080efbe3e4a1430ba0671f2e43a202bf45b05479cd", "a3894003ad1d293ba96d77881ccd2071446dc3f65f434669b49b3da92421901a"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Defending SaaS-based applications against ShinyHunters OAuth abuse

2026-07-13 15 use cases 9 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Microsoft Threat Intelligence identified threat actor activity with overlapping tradecraft commonly associated with ShinyHunters, including voice phishing (vishing), supply-chain compromise, and misconfigured guest access targeting SaaS-based applications.
