Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender · Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] First-seen Salesforce Connected App performing bulk API / report export (fake Data Loader) · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Salesforce Connected App API activity from ShinyHunters integration-abuse IPs · [LLM] Anomalous Salesforce ReportExport volume — bulk CRM exfiltration · [LLM] Guest-user Aura/GraphQL mass data retrieval from ShinyHunters IOC IP · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
Salesforce Connected App API activity from ShinyHunters integration-abuse IPs AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts Salesforce API/CRM query activity attributed to a Connected App originating from the specific source IPs Microsoft tied to ShinyHunters/UNC6395 abuse of trusted OAuth integrations (Salesloft Drift, Gainsight, Klue). Because the actors ride sanctioned OAuth tokens, IP is the highest-fidelity anchor available on this telemetry. Rationale: Anchors on the five Microsoft-published IOC IPs (article Table 2; 138.226.246.94 is explicitly the Klue integration performing CRM API queries) scoped to Salesforce API/Connected-App activity — a fixed IP set on SaaS API telemetry is an alerting-grade match with near-zero legitimate overlap. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/data-theft-salesforce-instances-via-salesloft-drift • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/microsoft-maps-year-long-shinyhunters.html
ATT&CKT1199 T1550.001
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate integration vendor (Klue/Gainsight) re-uses one of these IPs post-remediation for sanctioned traffic
  • Corporate egress NAT coincidentally shares an IP block with a listed address
  • Threat-intel enrichment jobs or a SOC replay hitting the Salesforce API from a sinkholed IP
  • Security researcher / IR team validating the IOC against the tenant
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull all CloudAppEvents for the matched IP, note the ConnectedAppId and AccountDisplayName acting on its behalf, and confirm whether the app is an approved Salesloft/Gainsight/Klue integration. 2) Contain: in Salesforce, revoke the Connected App's OAuth tokens and block the source IP at the org login-IP-range/Connected-App policy; rotate the integration's connection secret. 3) Hunt: enumerate every ReportExport/BulkApi call by that ConnectedAppId, pivot to other tenants/users the same app touched, and search for the remaining four IOC IPs and any credentials exposed in exported records.
let IocIps = dynamic(["138.226.246.94","212.86.125.24","213.111.148.90","94.154.32.160"]);
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where Application == "Salesforce"
| where IPAddress in (IocIps)
| extend ConnectedAppId = tostring(coalesce(RawEventData.CONNECTED_APP_ID, RawEventData.ConnectedAppId))
| summarize Events=count(), Actions=make_set(ActionType,10), ConnectedApps=make_set(ConnectedAppId,10), Users=make_set(AccountDisplayName,10), UAs=make_set(UserAgent,10), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp) by IPAddress, ISP, CountryCode
| order by Events desc

First-seen Salesforce Connected App performing bulk API / report export (fake Data Loader) AIInstallation Medium
Surfaces a Connected App ID that has never been observed in the tenant baseline suddenly issuing API calls or report exports — the pattern left by ShinyHunters' vishing-driven OAuth consent to a malicious app disguised as the legitimate Salesforce Data Loader. Catches consent-phishing even when the source IP is not a known IOC. Rationale: Uses the article's own ConnectedAppId extraction (RawEventData.CONNECTED_APP_ID / ConnectedAppId, code Block 1) but replaces the non-schema UncommonForUser flag with a 30-day first-seen anti-join — a newly-consented app doing bulk API/export is exactly the malicious 'Data Loader' behaviour Microsoft describes. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/microsoft-maps-year-long-shinyhunters.html • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/data-theft-salesforce-instances-via-salesloft-drift
ATT&CKT1528 T1550.001
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate new integration onboarded by IT during the lookback window (e.g. a sanctioned analytics or backup app)
  • Salesforce Data Loader genuinely used by an admin for a one-off migration
  • Connected App re-registered with a new ID after a secret rotation
  • Sandbox-to-prod app promotion generating a first-seen ID
Suppression filter
| where UAs has_any ("python","Salesforce-","Bulk API","axios","node-fetch","Go-http-client") or Events > 500  // narrow to automated bulk-access user-agents / high volume
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the ConnectedApp's granted OAuth scopes and the consenting user; check whether the consent event correlates with a help-desk/vishing report or an unusual admin session. 2) Contain: revoke the app's tokens, remove the Connected App, and force-reauth/reset the consenting user if a scope like api or full was granted. 3) Hunt: list every record type queried/exported by the app, cross-reference the five IOC IPs, and review other users who consented to the same app name across the tenant.

Anomalous Salesforce ReportExport volume — bulk CRM exfiltration AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects a Salesforce user identity exporting reports at a volume far above normal, the mass-exfiltration step Microsoft observed across all three ShinyHunters intrusion paths (accounts, contacts, and service-case data pulled at scale). Pivots on Salesforce report-export events rather than authentication, which the actors evade. Rationale: Built directly on the article's ReportExport code (Block 2, RawEventData.USER_ID) and Microsoft's 'Possible Salesforce scraping activity' coverage; a per-hour export burst is the concrete exfiltration signal for accounts/contacts/case data the actors bulk-queried. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/data-theft-salesforce-instances-via-salesloft-drift • https://www.mitiga.io/blog/shinyhunters-and-unc6395-inside-the-salesforce-and-salesloft-breaches
ATT&CKT1567 T1213
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Quarterly business-review or finance close where an analyst legitimately exports many reports
  • A scheduled BI/ETL service account performing routine bulk report pulls
  • Data-migration or Salesforce backup job running as a user identity
  • Sales-ops power user building a large territory dataset
Suppression filter
| where not (AccountDisplayName has_any ("svc","integration","backup","etl") and UAs has_any ("Salesforce Reporting","DataLoader","Informatica"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the SalesforceUserId is a human, an integration/service account, or a hijacked session; compare the export IPs/user-agents against the five IOC IPs and the user's normal geo. 2) Contain: suspend the Salesforce session/user and revoke associated OAuth grants; enable/verify Salesforce Shield Event Monitoring transaction security to block further exports. 3) Hunt: enumerate the specific reports/objects exported, assess data sensitivity, and pivot to Connected-App attribution to see if the exports rode a compromised integration token.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Salesforce"
| where ActionType == "ReportExport"
| extend SalesforceUserId = tostring(RawEventData.USER_ID)
| summarize Exports=count(), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), IPs=make_set(IPAddress,10), UAs=make_set(UserAgent,10) by bin(Timestamp, 1h), AccountObjectId, AccountId, AccountDisplayName, SalesforceUserId
| where Exports > 50   // 50 exports/hr >> typical per-user report cadence; empirical bulk-exfil threshold
| order by Exports desc

Guest-user Aura/GraphQL mass data retrieval from ShinyHunters IOC IP AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts unauthenticated guest-user Salesforce activity from IOC IP 103.75.11.78 (Microsoft: targeting the Aura framework via guest access, 19–22 June), where chained Aura/GraphQL requests circumvented record-retrieval limits to scrape data far beyond normal guest scope. Targets the misconfigured-guest-access intrusion path. Rationale: Anchors on the single IOC IP Microsoft attributes specifically to Aura-framework guest-access data theft (Table 2, 19–22 June window) and surfaces the guest/USER_TYPE context — a fixed IP tied to a named intrusion path makes this alerting-grade and distinct from the integration-IP UC. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/microsoft-maps-year-long-shinyhunters.html • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/data-theft-salesforce-instances-via-salesloft-drift
ATT&CKT1213 T1078.004
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A vulnerability scanner or bug-bounty researcher probing the org's Experience Cloud / Aura endpoints from that IP after IOC publication
  • Legitimate high-volume anonymous community-portal browsing sharing the IP via CGNAT
  • IR/pentest engagement replaying the Aura request chain for validation
  • Third-party uptime monitor hitting public community pages
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the activity is guest/unauthenticated (USER_TYPE) and enumerate the Aura/GraphQL endpoints and objects returned; determine which guest-exposed records were reachable. 2) Contain: tighten guest-user object/field permissions and sharing rules on the affected Experience Cloud site, disable unauthenticated Aura endpoints not required, and block the IP. 3) Hunt: review all guest-user activity across community sites for chained Aura/GraphQL scraping patterns and abnormally large result sets, and check for the same IP against the other Salesforce intrusion paths.

| summarize Requests=count(), Actions=make_set(ActionType,15), UserTypes=make_set(UserType,5), Accounts=make_set(AccountDisplayName,10), UAs=make_set(UserAgent,10), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp) by IPAddress, ISP, CountryCode

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator Delivery High
External Teams chat where displayName contains 'helpdesk' or 'IT support' — common 2024+ vishing pattern (Storm-1811, Black Basta, UNC6692). No CIM data model maps to Teams chats; uses raw O365 audit logs.
ATT&CKT1566.004 T1566
Data sourcesCloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType == "MessageSent"
| where RawEventData has "ExternalParticipants"
| extend SenderDisplayName = tostring(parse_json(RawEventData).SenderDisplayName)
| where SenderDisplayName matches regex @"(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, ActivityType, SenderDisplayName, RawEventData
// External Teams chat — Teams audit lives in OfficeActivity.
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "MicrosoftTeams"
| where Operation in~ ("MessageSent","ChatCreated","TeamsImpersonationDetected")
| where isnotempty(UserId)
| where Subject has_any ("IT","helpdesk","support","password","verify")
   or Recipients has_any ("IT","helpdesk")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, Operation, Subject, Recipients,
          ClientIP, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
`o365_management_activity`
  Workload=MicrosoftTeams Operation=MessageSent
  ExternalParticipants=*
| where match(SenderDisplayName, "(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)")
| stats count, earliest(_time) as firstTime, latest(_time) as lastTime
    by SenderUpn, SenderDisplayName, RecipientUpn, ChatId

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High

DeviceEvents

SecurityEvent

| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"

Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] DIRAC FileCatalog checkDataset SQL injection carrying Python eval gadget (CVE-2026-61667)

Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.

Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Post-RCE read of DIRAC dirac.cfg / proxy / token stores on FileCatalog host · [LLM] DIRAC dirac.cfg/proxy access followed by outbound egress from service process (exfiltration) · [LLM] DIRAC service process deletes or truncates its own logs (anti-forensics post-RCE)
DIRAC FileCatalog checkDataset SQL injection carrying Python eval gadget (CVE-2026-61667) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts DIRAC FileCatalog / DatasetManager service logs for checkDataset requests whose datasets parameter contains SQL-injection tokens (UNION/SELECT/quote-break) combined with a Python eval gadget (__import__/os.system/subprocess). This is the exact CVE-2026-61667 vector where the injected SQL result is passed straight to eval() for RCE. Rationale: Uses the article's named function `checkDataset` and `DatasetManager` FileCatalog components plus the eval-gadget strings an attacker must return through the SQLi (__import__/os.system) — a combination that never appears in a benign dataset name. Defender/Falcon left empty because DIRAC application/DB logs are not shipped to Defender XDR or the Falcon FDR. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-m4m7-4cw8-62j6 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/dirac/CVE-2026-61667/ • https://dailycve.com/dirac-filecatalog-datasetmanager-remote-code-execution-rce-via-sql-injection-eval-cve-2026-61667-critical-dc-jul2026-956/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A pentester or vuln-scanner (e.g. sqlmap) probing the FileCatalog endpoint during an authorized assessment
  • Developer/QA testing dataset queries containing literal words like 'union' or 'select' in a legitimate dataset name
  • DIRAC integration tests that intentionally exercise malformed dataset inputs
  • A security researcher validating the CVE-2026-61667 patch on a staging node
Suppression filter
| where not (SyslogMessage has_any ("sqlmap","pytest","integration-test","unittest"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full request/log line and the authenticated user identity; confirm the datasets value contains both SQL syntax and a Python gadget (not just the word 'union'). Check the DIRAC version against patched 8.0.79 / 9.0.22 / 9.1.10. 2) Contain: revoke the offending user's DIRAC proxy/token, isolate the FileCatalog host from egress, and snapshot service logs before the attacker can prune them. 3) Hunt: on the same host look for python-service→shell spawns (UC2), reads of dirac.cfg (UC3), and outbound exfil (UC4) within the same session window.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ProcessName has_any ("dirac","FileCatalog","DataManagement","tornado")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("checkDataset","DatasetManager","FileCatalog")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("UNION","__import__","os.system","subprocess","commands.getoutput","eval(")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("'","\"","--","/*",";")   // quote-break / statement-stack markers
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:linux.syslog (@process.name:*dirac* OR @process.name:*FileCatalog* OR @process.name:*tornado*) AND (checkDataset OR DatasetManager) AND (UNION OR __import__ OR os.system OR subprocess)

| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

DIRAC FileCatalog service Python process spawns shell or recon binary (eval RCE) AIInstallation High
Flagship post-exploitation detection for CVE-2026-61667: the DIRAC FileCatalog/DatasetManager service Python process (which calls eval on attacker-controlled DB output) spawning /bin/sh, bash or reconnaissance tools. Legitimately the FileCatalog service never forks a shell. Rationale: Pairs the article's named service components (FileCatalog/DatasetManager parent Python cmdline) with shell/recon children — the exact behaviour a passed-to-eval() gadget produces. Datadog/Falcon can't see the DIRAC parent cmdline (auditd EXECVE and the ProcessRollup2 reference lack parent-cmdline), so those variants scope to recon children only and are noisier — hence tier alerting rests on the Defender/Sentinel/Splunk parent-aware forms. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-m4m7-4cw8-62j6 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/dirac/CVE-2026-61667/
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A DIRAC administrator running maintenance scripts that legitimately shell out from a python service wrapper
  • DIRAC agents that call subprocess to invoke gfal/xrootd data-transfer CLIs during normal operation
  • Monitoring/health-check plugins that run 'uname'/'id' from the service context
  • Container entrypoint scripts where python launches bash during startup
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("gfal","xrdcp","xrootd","healthcheck","/usr/libexec/"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child process command line and full process tree — a benign gfal transfer looks nothing like 'sh -c id;curl'. Confirm the parent is the FileCatalog/DatasetManager service and identify the authenticated caller from correlated service logs (UC1). 2) Contain: kill the child process, isolate the host from egress, and freeze the DIRAC service user's proxies/tokens. 3) Hunt: check for dirac.cfg reads (UC3), outbound exfil (UC4) and log tampering (UC5) tied to the same PID/session.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("python","python3")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("FileCatalog","DatasetManager","dirac-service","tornado-start","DIRAC")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","id","whoami","uname","curl","wget","nc","ncat","cat","chmod","python","python3")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("python","python3")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("FileCatalog","DatasetManager","dirac-service","tornado-start","DIRAC")
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("sh","bash","dash","id","whoami","uname","curl","wget","nc","ncat","cat","chmod","python")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Post-RCE read of DIRAC dirac.cfg / proxy / token stores on FileCatalog host AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts for a shell/python child of the DIRAC service reading or exporting dirac.cfg (which holds DB passwords) or the proxy/token stores — the article's stated objective once RCE is achieved. Scopes to file-access binaries operating on DIRAC config/credential paths. Rationale: Anchored on the article's explicit loot list — 'read the local dirac.cfg, get database passwords and export all stored proxies and tokens' — via the concrete dirac.cfg filename and DIRAC config/proxy paths. Medium FP because admins do legitimately read dirac.cfg; the shell/python parent constraint keeps it tight. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-m4m7-4cw8-62j6 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/dirac/CVE-2026-61667/
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A DIRAC sysadmin manually cat-ing dirac.cfg during troubleshooting from an interactive shell
  • Backup/config-management jobs (Ansible, rsync, tar) archiving /opt/dirac/etc
  • Legitimate dirac-proxy-init / dirac-admin tooling touching the proxy store
  • Monitoring agents parsing dirac.cfg for health metrics
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("ansible","rsync","dirac-proxy-init","dirac-admin") or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("sshd","sudo"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: determine whether the reader's parent is an interactive admin login or the FileCatalog service; the latter is the true positive. Cross-reference the timestamp with UC1/UC2 hits for the same host/user. 2) Contain: rotate the database credentials stored in dirac.cfg and revoke ALL proxies/tokens the service could export — assume they are compromised. 3) Hunt: look for outbound transfer of that data (UC4) and for reuse of the exported proxies/tokens against external grid resources.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("dirac.cfg","/opt/dirac/etc","dirac-proxy","ProxyDB","proxyDB","export") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("dirac.cfg","/opt/dirac","proxy","token")
| where FileName in~ ("cat","grep","less","more","head","tail","strings","base64","xxd","tar","scp","python","python3")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("python","python3","sh","bash","dash")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("cat","grep","less","head","tail","strings","base64","xxd","tar","scp","python","python3")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("dirac.cfg","/opt/dirac/etc","dirac-proxy","ProxyDB","proxyDB")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("python","python3","sh","bash","dash")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

DIRAC dirac.cfg/proxy access followed by outbound egress from service process (exfiltration) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Correlates a read/export of dirac.cfg or the proxy/token store (UC3 vector) with an outbound public network connection from a python/shell process on the same host within 10 minutes — the exfiltration step that turns credential theft into loss. Directly maps the article's 'export all stored proxies and tokens' impact. Rationale: Two-stage correlation (credential read → outbound egress from the same host, same process class, ≤10 min) captures the article's proxy/token exfil impact without a static IOC. No Sigma/Datadog — the detection is a cross-event temporal join those single-event shapes can't express. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-m4m7-4cw8-62j6 • https://dailycve.com/dirac-filecatalog-datasetmanager-remote-code-execution-rce-via-sql-injection-eval-cve-2026-61667-critical-dc-jul2026-956/
ATT&CKT1041 T1552.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • DIRAC service legitimately fetching config then making outbound grid data transfers (gfal/xrootd) to public endpoints
  • Config-management pulling dirac.cfg then syncing to a remote repo/artifact store
  • Backup jobs tar-ing /opt/dirac and shipping it to off-site storage over scp/sftp
  • Monitoring agent reading config then POSTing metrics to a SaaS collector
Suppression filter
| where RemoteUrl !has_any ("xrootd","gfal","srm","eos") and RemotePort !in (1094, 2811, 8443)
Response runbook
1) Triage: examine the outbound destination — a known grid SE/xrootd endpoint is likely benign; an unfamiliar cloud IP/paste site is not. Confirm the preceding config/proxy read was by the service, not an admin. 2) Contain: block the destination at egress, rotate dirac.cfg DB credentials, and revoke every proxy/token in the store. 3) Hunt: check the destination IP for reuse across other DIRAC hosts and pivot on the exported proxies being replayed against external resources.
let Window = 10m;
let CfgAccess = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("dirac.cfg","dirac-proxy","ProxyDB","/opt/dirac/etc")
    | where FileName in~ ("cat","grep","python","python3","tar","base64","scp","curl")
    | project CfgTime = Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, CfgCmd = ProcessCommandLine;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python","python3","curl","wget","scp","sftp","bash","sh","nc","ncat")
| join kind=inner CfgAccess on DeviceName
| where Timestamp between (CfgTime .. CfgTime + Window)
| project CfgTime, NetTime = Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, CfgCmd, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by NetTime desc
let Window = 10m;
let CfgAccess = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("dirac.cfg","dirac-proxy","ProxyDB","/opt/dirac/etc")
    | project CfgTime = TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, CfgCmd = TargetProcessCommandLine;
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where NetworkDirection == "Outbound"
| where SrcUsername != "" or isnotempty(DstIpAddr)
| join kind=inner CfgAccess on DvcHostname
| where TimeGenerated between (CfgTime .. CfgTime + Window)
| project CfgTime, NetTime = TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, CfgCmd, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url
| order by NetTime desc

DIRAC service process deletes or truncates its own logs (anti-forensics post-RCE) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the DIRAC FileCatalog service (or its shell child) deleting, shredding or truncating DIRAC log files — the article's noted capability to 'remove evidence of the exploit from the log' after achieving RCE. Scopes to file-destruction binaries targeting DIRAC log paths. Rationale: Grounded in the article's stated anti-forensics capability ('remove evidence of the exploit from the log'), constrained to DIRAC log paths plus a python/shell parent so it doesn't fire on generic logrotate. Medium confidence because attacker log paths vary; the parent-process constraint is the fidelity anchor. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-m4m7-4cw8-62j6 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/dirac/CVE-2026-61667/
ATT&CKT1070.002 T1070.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • logrotate or a cron cleanup job pruning old DIRAC logs (parent would be cron/logrotate, not python service)
  • A DIRAC admin manually clearing a noisy log during troubleshooting
  • CI/CD or container rebuild wiping /opt/dirac logs on redeploy
  • Disk-space remediation scripts truncating large .log files
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("logrotate","cron","crond","anacron","systemd")
Response runbook
1) Triage: verify the deleting process's parent — logrotate/cron is benign, the FileCatalog service Python or an interactive attacker shell is not. Recover deleted logs from backup/journald if possible. 2) Contain: preserve remaining forensic artifacts (auditd, EDR raw events, memory) immediately since local logs may be gone; isolate the host. 3) Hunt: reconstruct the intrusion from EDR/auditd (which the attacker cannot prune) — correlate with UC1 (SQLi), UC2 (RCE) and UC3 (credential read) to establish the full chain and blast radius.

| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("rm","shred","truncate","unlink","sed")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/opt/dirac","dirac","FileCatalog") and ProcessCommandLine has_any (".log","/log/","ServiceLog","serverlog")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("python","python3","sh","bash","dash")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("rm","shred","truncate","unlink","sed")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("/opt/dirac","dirac","FileCatalog")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any (".log","/log/","ServiceLog","serverlog")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("python","python3","sh","bash","dash")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).

DIRAC ReqManager service (CVE-2026-45579) spawning a shell or recon/egress binary AIExploitation High
Hunts the RCE payload executing: the DIRAC RequestManager service (a Python DB-facing handler launched via dirac-service/dirac-tornado as ReqManager/TornadoReqManager) spawning /bin/sh, bash or a recon/egress tool. The eval() on the unrecognised groupingAttribute walks back to the os module, so successful exploitation manifests as this DB service forking a shell — something ReqManager never does legitimately (unlike RequestExecutingAgent, which forks a ProcessPool). Rationale: Anchored on the ReqManager/ReqManagerHandler/dirac-service parent identity (DIRAC docs: ReqManager is the DB-facing handler that never shells out) combined with any shell/recon/egress child — the exact tree the eval()->os.* chain from the advisory produces. Parent token deliberately excludes RequestExecutingAgent, which forks a legitimate ProcessPool. Datadog/Falcon left empty: their provided auditd/ProcessRollup2 schemas expose no parent command line to key the DIRAC-service parent on (only ParentBaseFileName='python', too generic). Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/dirac/CVE-2026-45579/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9jpv-c7p4-997x • https://dirac.diracgrid.org/en/latest/AdministratorGuide/Systems/RequestManagement/rmsComponents.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • DIRAC administrator running diagnostic shell commands under the runit/supervisor process tree during service troubleshooting
  • Container entrypoint/init wrapper spawning a shell during a dirac-service (re)start
  • Config-management (Ansible/Puppet/Salt) restarting dirac-tornado and running post-restart health-check shell hooks
  • Site monitoring probes (monit/nagios) that shell out from the service supervisor
  • A local health-check script using curl/nc to poll the ReqManager port on service start
Suppression filter
| where ChildCmd !has "healthcheck" and ChildCmd !has "/opt/dirac/pro/versions" and ChildCmd !has "runsvdir"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the child command line and SHA256; correlate against the ReqManager log for the exception traceback the advisory says the exploit leaves (NameError/AttributeError referencing 'Request.' or dunder strings such as __class__/__globals__/__builtins__), and identify the authenticated user whose RPC to getRequestCountersWeb preceded it. 2) Contain: isolate the DIRAC host, rotate all secrets in dirac.cfg (database passwords) and revoke every stored proxy/token, then upgrade DIRAC to 8.0.79 / 9.0.22 / 9.1.10. 3) Hunt: search the same host for reads of dirac.cfg by non-DIRAC processes, outbound egress from the service, and truncation/deletion of the RequestManager log (evidence removal noted in the advisory).

| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("dirac-service","dirac-tornado","ReqManagerHandler","ReqManager")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","ksh","curl","wget","nc","ncat","socat","id","whoami","hostname","uname","cat","base64","chmod")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("dirac-service","dirac-tornado","ReqManagerHandler","ReqManager")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("/sh","/bash","/dash","/zsh","/ksh","/curl","/wget","/nc","/ncat","/socat","/id","/whoami","/hostname","/uname","/cat","/base64","/chmod")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

DIRAC post-exploit read of dirac.cfg by a shell/read utility (CVE-2026-45579 credential theft) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the credential-theft step the advisory describes: after the eval() RCE, the attacker reads the local dirac.cfg to harvest database passwords and export stored proxies/tokens. Keys on a read/exfil utility (cat, grep, base64, curl, etc.) whose own command line references dirac.cfg — excluding the Python DIRAC service that carries dirac.cfg as a legitimate --cfg argument. Rationale: Keys on dirac.cfg (the file the advisory names as holding DB passwords and gating proxy/token export) appearing in the command line of a read/exfil utility rather than the Python service. The reader-binary allowlist excludes the legitimate DIRAC process, which carries dirac.cfg as a --cfg argument — so any cat/grep/base64/curl of dirac.cfg is anomalous. Portable across all process-telemetry platforms because it keys on the executing process's own command line. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/dirac/CVE-2026-45579/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9jpv-c7p4-997x
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1552.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • DIRAC administrator manually running cat/grep on dirac.cfg during troubleshooting over SSH
  • Backup jobs (tar/rsync driven via cat) reading the DIRAC etc/ directory
  • Config-management tooling templating or diffing dirac.cfg on each run
  • Monitoring/inventory scripts grepping dirac.cfg for a version or option value
  • Site install/upgrade scripts copying dirac.cfg with scp/curl to a new node
Suppression filter
and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("dirac-service","dirac-tornado","ReqManagerHandler","ReqManager")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the parent of the reader process — if it descends from the DIRAC service (dirac-service/dirac-tornado/ReqManager) rather than an interactive admin shell, treat as confirmed exploitation; check whether the command pipes to base64/curl/nc (exfil) and whether stored proxy/token files were touched. 2) Contain: isolate the host, immediately rotate every credential in dirac.cfg and revoke all stored user proxies and tokens, and patch DIRAC to 8.0.79 / 9.0.22 / 9.1.10. 3) Hunt: pivot on the authenticated user who called getRequestCountersWeb, review the ReqManager log for the eval exception traceback, and look for outbound transfers of dirac.cfg / proxy material and any subsequent log truncation.

| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "dirac.cfg"
| where FileName in~ ("cat","grep","egrep","less","more","head","tail","base64","od","strings","xxd","curl","wget","scp","nc","ncat")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

npm maintainer credential-phish lookalike domain npmjs.help (chalk/debug ATO) AIDelivery High
Hunts endpoint DNS/web contact to the lookalike domain npmjs.help, the fake '2FA reset' phishing site used to steal the npm maintainer credentials behind the September 2025 chalk/debug supply-chain compromise. Legitimate npm lives on npmjs.com/npmjs.org, so any hit on npmjs.help is a maintainer-targeted credential-phishing indicator. Rationale: npmjs.help is a confirmed lookalike phishing domain (registered 2025-09-05, three days pre-attack) named in the article and corroborated by Sygnia/Checkmarx/Cycode/Aikido as the credential-theft vector for the chalk/debug ATO. Exact-domain match against a domain with no legitimate use = high fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/npm-debug-and-chalk-packages-compromised • https://www.sygnia.co/threat-reports-and-advisories/npm-supply-chain-attack-september-2025/ • https://checkmarx.com/zero-post/chalk-and-17-other-npm-packages-compromised-in-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1656
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SOC analyst or TI platform detonating/browsing npmjs.help in a sandboxed research VM
  • Automated URL-enrichment (SOAR/secure-web-gateway) resolving the domain for reputation scoring
  • Security-awareness phishing-simulation platform hosting a lookalike test page
  • DNS sinkhole/RPZ appliance logging the blocked query
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the host/user that resolved npmjs.help and whether a browser or npm tooling initiated it; pull any credential-entry or npm login activity in the following 30 min. 2) Contain: force-reset the affected npm account credentials and revoke/rotate npm publish tokens and 2FA; block npmjs.help at the proxy/DNS. 3) Hunt: check whether that maintainer published any npm package versions after the resolution timestamp, and scan lockfiles/CI for the chalk/debug malicious versions and browser-side crypto-address-swapping payloads.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "npmjs.help"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has "npmjs.help"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

plain-crypto-js postinstall RAT dropper spawns downloader (axios/Sapphire Sleet) AIInstallation High
Hunts the malicious plain-crypto-js@4.2.1 postinstall (setup.js) hook — pulled in transitively by axios@1.14.1/0.30.4 — spawning a downloader/interpreter that references the RAT campaign artifacts (sfrclak C2, campaign ID 6202033) to fetch platform-specific payloads. Targets the exact execution behaviour Microsoft attributes to Sapphire Sleet. Rationale: sfrclak, 142.11.206.73, campaign ID 6202033 and the plain-crypto-js dependency name are Datadog/Elastic/Socket-confirmed IOCs for the March 2026 axios RAT dropper (setup.js postinstall). These strings do not appear in benign build output, making a command-line match high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/axios-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/04/01/mitigating-the-axios-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://socket.dev/blog/axios-npm-package-compromised
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059 T1105

  • IR/hunt scripts that embed the IOC strings as search arguments in their own command lines
  • Threat-intel simulation/purple-team replay of the axios TTPs
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("windbg.exe","procmon.exe") or DeviceName has_any ("MALWARE-LAB","SANDBOX"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the parent chain (node.exe/npm → interpreter) and whether the host has axios 1.14.1/0.30.4 or plain-crypto-js 4.2.1 in node_modules/lockfiles. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the RAT chain, and block sfrclak[.]com + 142.11.206.73 at egress. 3) Hunt: sweep for the dropped artifacts (%PROGRAMDATA%\wt.exe, system.bat, %TEMP%\6202033.ps1/.vbs, /Library/Caches/com.apple.act.mond, /tmp/ld.py), the MicrosoftUpdate Run key, and beacons to the C2; rotate any dev/CI credentials on the machine.

axios RAT dropped artifacts: renamed PowerShell wt.exe + campaign 6202033 files AIInstallation High
Hunts file-system writes of the axios/plain-crypto-js RAT's dropped payloads across OSes: a renamed PowerShell (%PROGRAMDATA%\wt.exe), the persistence script system.bat, VBScript/PS1 droppers named 6202033, the macOS fake Apple daemon com.apple.act.mond, and the Linux payload ld.py. These paths are masquerading indicators unique to the Sapphire Sleet RAT staging. Rationale: The dropped paths (%PROGRAMDATA%\wt.exe = renamed PowerShell, system.bat, %TEMP%\6202033.ps1/.vbs, /Library/Caches/com.apple.act.mond, /tmp/ld.py) are verbatim IOCs from Datadog/Elastic write-ups. Excluding \WindowsApps\ removes the legitimate Windows Terminal wt.exe, leaving only the masqueraded copy. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/axios-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/axios-one-rat-to-rule-them-all • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/axios-compromised-on-npm-malicious-versions-drop-remote-access-trojan

Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment

  • An admin/backup script legitimately named system.bat deployed via GPO to ProgramData
  • A developer repo on macOS/Linux containing an unrelated ld.py linker helper
  • EDR sample-collection/quarantine copying the artifact into a scan folder
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath !has @"\WindowsApps\" and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("gpscript.exe","msiexec.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the writing process (should trace back to node.exe/npm postinstall) and hash the dropped file against the published SHA-256s (e.g. Windows PS payload 617b67a8e1210e4fc87c92d1d1da45a2f311c08d26e89b12307cf583c900d101). 2) Contain: isolate host, delete artifacts, remove the MicrosoftUpdate Run key, block sfrclak[.]com/142.11.206.73. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same InitiatingProcess across the fleet, and audit npm lockfiles org-wide for axios 1.14.1/0.30.4 and plain-crypto-js 4.2.1.

axios RAT persistence: HKCU Run value MicrosoftUpdate pointing to system.bat AIInstallation High
Hunts the exact autostart persistence set by the axios/plain-crypto-js RAT: an HKCU CurrentVersion\Run value named 'MicrosoftUpdate' whose data references system.bat, re-executing the payload at each logon. The masqueraded value name plus the system.bat data string make this a tight, single-event persistence signal. Rationale: The Run value name 'MicrosoftUpdate' -> system.bat is the exact persistence IOC documented by Datadog for the axios RAT. Value-name masquerading as a Microsoft component combined with a .bat data string is a precise, low-noise autostart indicator. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/axios-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/04/01/mitigating-the-axios-npm-supply-chain-compromise/
ATT&CKT1547.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate internal update tool that (poorly) names its Run value MicrosoftUpdate and points to a .bat wrapper
  • Sysadmin logon automation deployed via a system.bat referenced in a Run key
  • Software packaging/testing that seeds throwaway Run keys
  • Golden-image build tooling writing autostart entries
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the writing process and the full RegistryValueData path; confirm whether it points to %PROGRAMDATA%\system.bat. 2) Contain: remove the Run value, delete system.bat and the renamed wt.exe, isolate the host, block the C2. 3) Hunt: query the fleet for the same value name/data pair, correlate to hosts that recently ran npm installs of axios/plain-crypto-js, and check egress logs for sfrclak[.]com beacons on port 8000.

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "RegistryValueSet"
| where RegistryKey has @"\CurrentVersion\Run"
| where RegistryValueName =~ "MicrosoftUpdate"
| where RegistryValueData has "system.bat"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\CurrentVersion\Run"
| where RegistryValue =~ "MicrosoftUpdate"
| where RegistryValueData has "system.bat"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData
| order by TimeGenerated desc

axios RAT C2 beacon to sfrclak[.]com / 142.11.206.73:8000 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts endpoint DNS/network contact to the axios RAT command-and-control infrastructure sfrclak[.]com and 142.11.206.73 (payload URL http://sfrclak[.]com:8000/6202033, 60-second beacon loop). Single-indicator network match against dedicated, freshly registered attacker infrastructure. Rationale: sfrclak[.]com (registered 2026-03-30) and 142.11.206.73:8000 are the Datadog/Elastic-confirmed C2 for the axios RAT. Dedicated attacker infrastructure with no legitimate use yields a near-zero-FP network detection. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/axios-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/axios-one-rat-to-rule-them-all • https://thehackernews.com/2026/03/axios-supply-chain-attack-pushes-cross.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • TI enrichment/sandbox host resolving sfrclak[.]com for reputation scoring
  • Security researcher pcap replay of the campaign
  • DNS sinkhole/RPZ logging the query it just blocked
  • Passive-DNS collector mirroring the domain
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the beaconing process (expect powershell/python/curl descended from node) and beacon cadence (~60s). 2) Contain: isolate host, block sfrclak[.]com + 142.11.206.73 at the firewall/proxy, kill the process tree. 3) Hunt: sweep the fleet for any resolution of sfrclak[.]com, correlate to recent axios/plain-crypto-js installs and the MicrosoftUpdate Run-key persistence, and rotate credentials cached on impacted hosts.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "sfrclak.com" or RemoteIP == "142.11.206.73"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
(ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has "sfrclak.com"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, Indicator = DnsQuery)
| union (CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP == "142.11.206.73" or DestinationHostName has "sfrclak.com"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr = SourceIP, SrcHostname = SourceHostName, Indicator = strcat(DestinationIP, " ", DestinationHostName))
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Malicious postmark-mcp BCC email exfiltration to phan@giftshop[.]club AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts outbound mail silently BCC'd to phan@giftshop[.]club, the exfiltration address hard-coded into the trojanised postmark-mcp@1.0.16 npm MCP server (the first confirmed malicious MCP server on npm). Any recipient in the giftshop.club domain on org mail flow is a direct exfiltration indicator. Rationale: phan@giftshop[.]club is the verbatim BCC exfiltration address added in postmark-mcp@1.0.16, corroborated by Snyk/The Register/The Hacker News. It matches the article's pre-extracted IOC giftshop.club; any org mail with a giftshop.club recipient is high-fidelity exfiltration. Cross-checked against: • https://snyk.io/blog/malicious-mcp-server-on-npm-postmark-mcp-harvests-emails/ • https://thehackernews.com/2025/09/first-malicious-mcp-server-found.html • https://www.theregister.com/2025/09/29/postmark_mcp_server_code_hijacked/
ATT&CKT1114 T1020 T1195.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A genuine business contact who happens to use a giftshop.club address (verify domain legitimacy first)
  • A phishing/threat-intel test message deliberately addressed to the IOC domain
  • Mail-security detonation/replay tooling re-sending a captured malicious message
  • A distribution-list expansion that legitimately contains the address (should be treated as compromise, not FP)
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull all messages with a giftshop.club recipient, note the sending mailboxes/service principals and whether the send path involved an MCP server or automation. 2) Contain: block giftshop.club at mail flow, purge outbound copies, and audit dev workstations for the postmark-mcp npm package (any version >=1.0.16); remove it. 3) Hunt: inventory MCP servers/AI-agent tooling pulling from npm, review what those agents had access to (email, secrets), and rotate any credentials the exposed emails may have contained.
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RecipientEmailAddress endswith "giftshop.club" or SenderFromDomain =~ "giftshop.club"
| project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, EmailDirection, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation
| order by Timestamp desc
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where OfficeWorkload =~ "Exchange"
| where Recipients has "giftshop.club" or P2RecipientList has "giftshop.club"
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, Operation, ClientIP, Recipients, P2RecipientList
| order by TimeGenerated desc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Email.All_Email where (All_Email.recipient="*giftshop.club*" OR All_Email.recipient="phan@giftshop.club") by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.subject | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Email.All_Email where (All_Email.recipient="*giftshop.club*" OR All_Email.recipient="phan@giftshop.club") by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.subject | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02

    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:

date: 2026/05/02

            - '\pwsh.exe'

            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'

jscrambler npm package publishes malicious preinstall binary

StepSecurity
2026-07-12 13 use cases 5 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

On July 11, 2026, version 8.14.0 of jscrambler was published to npm carrying a malicious preinstall hook that drops and executes a platform-specific native binary on Linux, Windows, and macOS. jscrambler is the official CLI client for the Jscrambler Code Integrity API, a commercial JavaScript obfuscation and web-app protection service, with a clean version history dating back to 0.1.0. The compromised release was flagged by StepSecurity's AI Release Analyzer with a suspicion score of 0 (the maximum suspicion rating) on publish.

jscrambler npm supply-chain: malicious dist/intro.js binary container drop AIDelivery High
Hunts creation of the oversized dist/intro.js file inside node_modules/jscrambler — a 7.8 MB custom binary container (magic 1B 43 53 49 01) disguised as JavaScript that ships the IronWorm Rust stealer for the compromised 8.14.0/8.16.0/8.17.0/8.18.0/8.20.0 releases. The legitimate intro.js in a JS-obfuscation CLI is tiny, so a multi-MB file at this exact path is a direct install-time IOC. Rationale: Anchored on the exact path node_modules/jscrambler/dist/intro.js plus the ~7.8 MB size that the article and Socket both cite; the legitimate CLI's intro.js is only KB, making the size+path combination high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/jscrambler-supply-chain-attack • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/compromised-jscrambler-8140-npm-release.html • https://threatlabsnews.xcitium.com/blog/jscrambler-npm-package-backdoored-inside-the-ironworm-infostealer-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1036.008
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A future legitimate jscrambler release that genuinely bundles a large intro.js asset (unlikely for an obfuscation CLI but possible)
  • Security researcher intentionally downloading the malicious tarball into a sandbox node_modules for analysis
  • Backup/restore or file-sync tools re-writing an archived node_modules tree containing the malicious file
  • EDR re-scanning a quarantined copy of node_modules causing a duplicate FileCreated event
Suppression filter
| where FileSize > 5000000
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the installed jscrambler version from package-lock.json / node_modules/jscrambler/package.json — flag if it is 8.14.0, 8.16.0, 8.17.0, 8.18.0 or 8.20.0. Compute SHA256 of dist/intro.js and match against the three payload hashes. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host; treat it as compromised. Kill any detached temp-dir process, remove node_modules, and downgrade to the last clean 8.13.0. Step 3 (hunt): Rotate every credential logged into a browser and all cloud/npm/GitHub tokens reachable from that host; pivot to UC4 to check for C2 callbacks to 37.27.122.124 / 57.128.246.79 and torproject endpoints.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FolderPath has @"\node_modules\jscrambler\dist\"
| where FileName =~ "intro.js"
| where FileSize > 5000000   // legit intro.js is tiny; the 8.14.0+ container is ~7.8 MB
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FolderPath, FileName, FileSize, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFilePath has @"\node_modules\jscrambler\dist\" or TargetFilePath has "/node_modules/jscrambler/dist/"
| where TargetFileName =~ "intro.js"
| where TargetFileSize > 5000000   // legit intro.js is tiny; container is ~7.8 MB
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSize, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
