IronWorm preinstall loader: detached hidden binary executed from OS temp by node.exe AIInstallation High
Hunts the jscrambler preinstall loader (dist/setup.js) decompressing the platform payload to a randomly named dotfile in the OS temp directory and spawning it detached from the npm install tree. The parent is node.exe and the child is a hidden `.<6+ alnum>.exe` in Temp — a shape almost nothing legitimate produces. Rationale: Combines the exact loader behaviour from the article — node.exe parent, randomly named dotfile (.[a-z0-9]{6,}) with .exe suffix, dropped and executed detached in the OS temp dir — into a parent+child+path signature that is specific to this preinstall stealer. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/jscrambler-supply-chain-attack • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/compromised-jscrambler-8140-npm-release.html
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1564.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Node-based build tools (electron-builder, node-gyp helpers) extracting signed helper executables to temp
  • Test frameworks that shell out to temporary compiled binaries during CI
  • A developer manually running a node script that writes a temp .exe with a dot-prefixed name
  • AV/EDR self-tests writing sample dotfiles to temp
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("electron-builder", "node-gyp"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Grab the child SHA256 and compare to the three IronWorm payload hashes; capture InitiatingProcessCommandLine to confirm it references jscrambler/dist/setup.js or intro.js. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, terminate the orphaned temp binary and any child processes, and block outbound to the known C2 IPs. Step 3 (hunt): Search DeviceNetworkEvents from that process for connections to 37.27.122.124 / 57.128.246.79 or *.torproject.org, and audit browser credential stores, MetaMask/Bitwarden vaults, and npm/GitHub tokens for theft.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node.exe"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\AppData\Local\Temp\", @"\Windows\Temp\", @"\Temp\")
| where FileName matches regex @"(?i)^\.[a-z0-9]{6,}\.exe$"   // random dotfile written by the loader
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\node.exe"
| where NewProcessName matches regex @"(?i)\\Temp\\\.[a-z0-9]{6,}\.exe$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, ParentProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

IronWorm cross-platform payload execution by SHA256 (jscrambler stealer binaries) AIInstallation Medium
High-fidelity hash-based alert for execution of the three extracted IronWorm payloads (ELF/PE32+/Mach-O) carried inside jscrambler dist/intro.js. Any match is a confirmed detonation of the stealer on the host. Rationale: Uses the three verified payload SHA256 values (Linux ELF, Windows PE32+, macOS Mach-O) from the IOC table; a hash match is a definitive TP with essentially zero legitimate collision. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/jscrambler-supply-chain-attack • https://threatlabsnews.xcitium.com/blog/jscrambler-npm-package-backdoored-inside-the-ironworm-infostealer-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware sample intentionally detonated in an approved analysis sandbox
  • EDR/AV scan events surfacing the hash without actual execution (image-load side)
  • Threat-intel enrichment tooling ingesting the sample file for hashing
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the event is real execution (not a scan) and identify the parent chain back to node.exe / npm. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host immediately, terminate the process, and preserve the temp binary for forensics. Step 3 (hunt): Enterprise-wide sweep for the same hashes and for jscrambler 8.14.0/8.16.0/8.17.0/8.18.0/8.20.0 in package-lock files; rotate all reachable cloud/npm/GitHub/AI-tool tokens and browser + wallet credentials.

IronWorm C2 beacon to hardcoded IPs and Tor endpoints from temp-dir process AICommand & Control Medium
Detects the IronWorm payload's command-and-control: direct connections to hardcoded IPs 37.27.122.124 and 57.128.246.79, plus Tor bootstrap to check.torproject.org / archive.torproject.org when initiated from the temp-dir loader. The two IPs are standalone high-fidelity; the Tor domains are gated on a temp-dir process to suppress legitimate Tor usage. Rationale: Uses the two hardcoded C2 IPs (confirmed by StepSecurity Harden-Runner and independently by Xcitium/Socket) as standalone signal, and gates the dual-use torproject.org bootstrap domains on a temp-dir initiating process to keep true legit Tor usage out. Cross-checked against: • https://threatlabsnews.xcitium.com/blog/jscrambler-npm-package-backdoored-inside-the-ironworm-infostealer-supply-chain-attack/ • https://socket.dev/blog/jscrambler-supply-chain-attack
ATT&CKT1090.003 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate developer/analyst intentionally running the Tor Browser or a Tor daemon on a workstation
  • Security research VM connecting to the C2 IPs during controlled detonation
  • Threat-intel scanner or sinkhole probing the same IPs from a monitored host
  • Shared-hosting reuse of 37.27.122.124 / 57.128.246.79 by a benign service after takedown (revalidate IP freshness periodically)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Temp\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\") or isempty(InitiatingProcessFolderPath) or RemoteIP in ("37.27.122.124", "57.128.246.79")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the initiating process — if it is a temp-dir dotfile .exe or a node.exe descendant, treat as confirmed IronWorm C2. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, block 37.27.122.124 and 57.128.246.79 at the egress firewall, and terminate the beaconing process. Step 3 (hunt): Correlate back to UC2/UC3 for the install and payload on the same host, pull any data staged for exfil, and rotate all cloud keys, npm/GitHub tokens, AI-tool/MCP API keys, and browser/wallet/Bitwarden credentials that were reachable.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("37.27.122.124", "57.128.246.79")
   or (RemoteUrl in~ ("check.torproject.org", "archive.torproject.org")
       and InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Temp\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\"))

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/

date: 2026/05/02

    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'

            - '\chrome.exe'

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02

    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1027

    - attack.defense-evasion

    category: process_creation
    product: windows

            - '\pwsh.exe'

            - '-enc '

            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'

            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'

falsepositives:

level: high

        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"

ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd") or SHA1 in~ ("fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd") or MD5 in~ ("fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd") or SHA1 in~ ("fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd") or MD5 in~ ("fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Injective npm Supply Chain Attack: 18 Packages Backdoored to Steal Crypto Wallet Keys

StepSecurity
2026-07-12 9 use cases 2 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

On July 8, 2026, attackers used access to a trusted developer's account to slip a backdoor into a widely used software development kit for the Injective blockchain. Disguised as harmless analytics, the code quietly captured wallet recovery phrases and private keys and sent them to an attacker-controlled server the moment a wallet was created or loaded. Automatic publishing pushed the tainted code out to 18 related packages within minutes, and it stayed live for less than an hour before being pulled and fixed. If your application installed any of the affected packages during that window, or pic…

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Injective npm Supply Chain Attack: 18 Packages Backdoored to Steal Crypto Wallet
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Backdoored @injectivelabs/sdk-ts 1.20.21 payload file dropped on disk · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Injective SDK wallet-key exfil to lookalike domain testnet.archival.chain.grpc-web.injective.network · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Injective SDK wallet-key exfil to lookalike domain testnet.archival.chain.grpc-web.injective.network AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts outbound resolution/connection to the attacker-controlled exfil host that the backdoored @injectivelabs/sdk-ts@1.20.21 reassembles from an obfuscated char-code array and POSTs stolen seed phrases / private keys to (carried base64 in the X-Request-Id header). The FQDN is a lookalike of legitimate Injective gRPC-Web infra but is not a real Injective endpoint, so exact-host contact is high fidelity. Rationale: Anchored on the exact FQDN testnet.archival.chain.grpc-web.injective.network decoded from the char-code array (_e/_d) in key-derivation-telemetry.ts; cross-checked against BleepingComputer, The Hacker News and SlowMist which all cite this host as the POST destination for the base64 secret in the X-Request-Id header. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/injective-sdk-on-npm-infected-with-cryptocurrency-wallet-stealer/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/injective-labs-github-compromise-pushes.html • https://slowmist.medium.com/threat-intelligence-injective-sdk-compromised-crypto-wallet-private-keys-stolen-0b8f06bf37ad • https://crypto.news/compromised-injective-sdk-sends-wallet-keys-through-fake-telemetry/
ATT&CKT1567 T1041 T1132.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer or CI runner still on the backdoored 1.20.21 build genuinely beaconing (this is a true positive, not an FP)
  • Malware sandbox / detonation VM replaying the sample and resolving the IOC
  • Threat-intel scanner or DNS sinkhole appliance resolving the indicator during enrichment
  • Security researcher manually curling the host to confirm it is live
Suppression filter
// scope to the SDK runtime to drop scanner/appliance noise
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","electron.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the resolving host and the initiating process (expect node.exe/electron.exe or a browser running a wallet/DEX frontend); pull the app's package-lock/node_modules to confirm @injectivelabs/sdk-ts@1.20.21 is present. 2) Contain: block the FQDN at proxy/DNS, isolate the host, and force-rotate every wallet seed phrase and private key that host touched — treat all as compromised. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host/user for the malicious file (key-derivation-telemetry / accounts-jQ1GSgaW.js), sweep the fleet for other hosts resolving the domain, and audit any downstream package pinning 1.20.21.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl =~ "testnet.archival.chain.grpc-web.injective.network"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name =~ "testnet.archival.chain.grpc-web.injective.network"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, ResultCode = ResultCodeName, ResolvedIPs = Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Backdoored @injectivelabs/sdk-ts 1.20.21 payload file dropped on disk AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the tainted SDK landing in node_modules on developer workstations, build agents, or servers via the distinctive payload filenames (key-derivation-telemetry.ts/.js, dist/esm/accounts-jQ1GSgaW.js) and the two published SHA256 hashes. These artifacts do not exist in the clean SDK, making on-disk presence unambiguous evidence of the compromised 1.20.21 release. Rationale: Uses the payload filenames from Stage 2 (key-derivation-telemetry.ts and compiled dist/esm/accounts-jQ1GSgaW.js) plus the two article-published SHA256 hashes — none of which exist in the clean 1.20.23 build — so any hit is a direct indicator of the tainted release rather than a behavioural heuristic. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/injective-sdk-on-npm-infected-with-cryptocurrency-wallet-stealer/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/injective-labs-github-compromise-pushes.html • https://slowmist.medium.com/threat-intelligence-injective-sdk-compromised-crypto-wallet-private-keys-stolen-0b8f06bf37ad

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02

            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'

            - '\Cookies'

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium

    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0", "9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9") or SHA1 in~ ("103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0", "9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9") or MD5 in~ ("103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0", "9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0", "9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9") or SHA1 in~ ("103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0", "9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9") or MD5 in~ ("103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0", "9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0", "9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Sha1-Hulud 2.0 npm worm payload files (setup_bun.js / bun_environment.js) written or executed · [LLM] Malicious 'SHA1HULUD' self-hosted GitHub Actions runner installation / persistence
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains

Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Cloud IMDS credential harvesting by node/npm/bun during package install (Sha1-Hulud/Megalodon) · [LLM] TruffleHog secret scanner spawned from an npm/bun package-install context (Sha1-Hulud) · [LLM] Sha1-Hulud destructive wiper fallback (cipher /W, recursive del, shred over home dir) · [LLM] CI/dev host exfiltrating to api.github.com shortly after cloud IMDS harvest (Sha1-Hulud exfil chain)
Sha1-Hulud 2.0 npm worm payload files (setup_bun.js / bun_environment.js) written or executed AIInstallation Medium
Hunts for the hardcoded self-propagating payload files the Sha1-Hulud/Megalodon npm worm drops during a malicious package preinstall, matched by exact filename and known SHA256. The article cites Sha1-Hulud dumping harvested credentials into public GitHub repos as the exfiltration destination it warns about; this catches the worm at the execution stage before that exfil happens. Rationale: Uses the exact worm payload filenames (setup_bun.js, bun_environment.js) and four published SHA256 hashes from Datadog/Microsoft analyses of Sha1-Hulud 2.0 — the campaign the article names as the archetype of GitHub-hosted secret exfiltration. Filename+hash makes this alerting-grade. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/12/09/shai-hulud-2-0-guidance-for-detecting-investigating-and-defending-against-the-supply-chain-attack/ • https://www.wiz.io/blog/shai-hulud-2-0-ongoing-supply-chain-attack
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher intentionally detonating a captured Sha1-Hulud sample in a sandbox VONM
  • Threat-intel/malware-repo mirror syncing sample files to a scanning host
  • EDR test/purple-team exercise seeding the named hashes
  • A benign project legitimately shipping a file literally named setup_bun.js (rare; hash filter avoids this)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe") or FolderPath has_any ("\\MalwareSamples\\","\\Quarantine\\"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the SHA256 matches a known worm hash and identify the InitiatingProcess (should be node/npm/bun preinstall). Pull the parent package name and package.json to find the poisoned dependency. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host/runner, revoke any npm/GitHub/cloud tokens present on it, and freeze the developer's npm publish rights. Step 3 (hunt): Search the org for the same hashes and for any public GitHub repos with description 'Sha1-Hulud: The Second Coming.'; rotate every secret reachable from the affected build.

Cloud IMDS credential harvesting by node/npm/bun during package install (Sha1-Hulud/Megalodon) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts for a JavaScript package-manager process (node, npm, bun, yarn, pnpm) reaching the cloud instance-metadata service (169.254.169.254 or metadata.google.internal) — the multi-cloud credential-harvest step of the Sha1-Hulud worm. This is the 'secret theft that never touches github.com' the article says public monitoring cannot see. Rationale: Combines the concrete IMDS endpoints (169.254.169.254, metadata.google.internal) documented by Datadog/Unit42 with the JS package-manager parent context that distinguishes worm harvesting from a legitimate cloud SDK call. Pins the abuse to the install-time process rather than any app. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/ • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/npm-supply-chain-attack/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/12/09/shai-hulud-2-0-guidance-for-detecting-investigating-and-defending-against-the-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1552.005 T1195.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A Node.js application running on an EC2/GCE instance that legitimately queries IMDS via the AWS/GCP SDK
  • Serverless/build tooling (e.g. serverless-framework, terraform-node wrappers) resolving instance credentials
  • Cloud-native CI agents written in Node fetching a metadata-scoped token for artifact upload
  • IMDSv2 token-refresh loops from a long-running node service
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("install","preinstall","postinstall","ci","npx") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "node_modules"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Determine whether the node/bun process was part of an npm/yarn install lifecycle (check parent chain and recent package.json changes) versus a steady-state application. Install-time IMDS access is the true positive. Step 2 (contain): Revoke the instance role's temporary credentials, quarantine the runner/host, and enforce IMDSv2 hop-limit=1 to block the container reach. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the host for setup_bun.js/bun_environment.js, trufflehog execution, and any subsequent api.github.com repo creation; rotate cloud keys the role could reach.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "169.254.169.254" or RemoteUrl has "metadata.google.internal"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","npm","npm.cmd","bun","bun.exe","yarn","pnpm")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ASCDeviceEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "169.254.169.254" or RemoteUrl has "metadata.google.internal"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","npm","npm.cmd","bun","bun.exe","yarn","pnpm")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by TimeGenerated desc

TruffleHog secret scanner spawned from an npm/bun package-install context (Sha1-Hulud) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts for the TruffleHog secret-discovery binary launched as a child of a JavaScript package manager or a shell inside an install script — the on-disk credential-sweep stage of the Sha1-Hulud worm. Distinct from sanctioned CI secret-scanning because the parent is node/npm/bun rather than a dedicated scanner job. Rationale: TruffleHog execution parented by node/bun/npm is the documented Sha1-Hulud secret-discovery step (Datadog/Wiz). The parent-process predicate separates worm-driven scans from an intentional trufflehog CI stage, keeping fidelity up. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/ • https://www.wiz.io/blog/shai-hulud-2-0-ongoing-supply-chain-attack
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A CI pipeline that legitimately runs trufflehog as a pre-commit/secret-scan step invoked from an npm script
  • Developer running `npx trufflehog` manually to audit a repo
  • Security tooling wrappers that shell out to trufflehog from a Node orchestrator
  • pre-commit framework invoking trufflehog via a node hook
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("pre-commit","secret-scan","security-scan","gitleaks-trufflehog-step"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm trufflehog was not a sanctioned pipeline step — inspect the initiating package.json script and whether the run coincides with an npm install rather than a scan job. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host/runner and revoke tokens; if part of a build, halt the pipeline and quarantine produced artifacts. Step 3 (hunt): Correlate with IMDS access, bun payload files, and outbound api.github.com repo creation on the same host; rotate any secrets trufflehog could have read.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName has "trufflehog" or ProcessCommandLine has "trufflehog"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","bun","bun.exe","npm","npm.cmd","yarn","pnpm","sh","bash")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has "trufflehog" or ActingProcessCommandLine has "trufflehog"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("node","bun","npm","yarn","pnpm","sh","bash")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Malicious 'SHA1HULUD' self-hosted GitHub Actions runner installation / persistence AIInstallation High
Hunts for the Sha1-Hulud worm registering an attacker-controlled self-hosted GitHub Actions runner — identified by the runner name SHA1HULUD, the $HOME/.dev-env install directory, RUNNER_ALLOW_RUNASROOT=1, and the actions-runner-linux-x64-2.330.0 download. This is the worm turning GitHub into a persistence/C2 channel, exactly the github.com-as-infrastructure abuse the article describes. Rationale: Pins on four hard, campaign-unique strings from Datadog's Sha1-Hulud 2.0 analysis (runner name SHA1HULUD, RUNNER_ALLOW_RUNASROOT=1, ~/.dev-env, actions-runner-linux-x64-2.330.0). These do not appear in legitimate runner setups, giving alerting-grade fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/12/09/shai-hulud-2-0-guidance-for-detecting-investigating-and-defending-against-the-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1543 T1102
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An org that coincidentally uses a self-hosted runner directory named .dev-env (unlikely, and runner-name string still filters it)
  • Admin legitimately setting RUNNER_ALLOW_RUNASROOT=1 in a container runner build (would lack the SHA1HULUD name)
  • Runner version 2.330.0 downloaded during a legitimate GitHub-hosted runner upgrade (string paired with the other markers reduces this)
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the runner registration name is SHA1HULUD or the install path is $HOME/.dev-env; check which GitHub org/repo the runner registered against. Step 2 (contain): Remove the runner from GitHub org settings, kill the runner process, revoke the PAT/GITHUB_TOKEN it used, and isolate the host. Step 3 (hunt): Search GitHub audit logs for self-hosted runner additions and for workflows triggered `on: discussion` with a `runs-on: self-hosted` job echoing github.event.discussion.body; enumerate other hosts with .dev-env.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("SHA1HULUD","RUNNER_ALLOW_RUNASROOT",".dev-env","actions-runner-linux-x64-2.330.0")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("SHA1HULUD","RUNNER_ALLOW_RUNASROOT",".dev-env","actions-runner-linux-x64-2.330.0")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Sha1-Hulud destructive wiper fallback (cipher /W, recursive del, shred over home dir) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts for the Sha1-Hulud worm's destructive fallback that fires when it cannot authenticate/propagate: on Windows `del /F /Q /S %USERPROFILE%` plus `cipher /W:%USERPROFILE%`, and on Linux `find $HOME ... | xargs shred -uvz`. High-impact, low-frequency behaviour that turns a supply-chain compromise into data destruction. Rationale: Encodes the exact destructive commands Datadog documented for Sha1-Hulud's failure path (`cipher /W:%USERPROFILE%`, `del /F /Q /S %USERPROFILE%*`, `find $HOME ... shred -uvz`). cipher /W over a user profile and shred over $HOME are near-zero in normal ops, making impact-stage alerting reliable. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/
ATT&CKT1485 T1070.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin/GPO running `cipher /W:` to wipe free space during decommissioning (usually not scoped to %USERPROFILE% and not spawned by node)
  • Backup or forensics tooling using shred for secure deletion of scratch data
  • A cleanup script using recursive del on a temp path (USERPROFILE token filter reduces this)
  • Disk-sanitisation compliance jobs
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","bun","bun.exe","sh","bash","cmd.exe","powershell.exe") or FileName =~ "cipher.exe"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the parent process — a wipe parented by node/bun/sh during an npm install is the true positive; capture the exact target path. Step 2 (contain): Immediately isolate the host from the network to stop further destruction and preserve volume shadow copies/backups; snapshot the disk. Step 3 (hunt): Confirm the Sha1-Hulud chain (bun payloads, trufflehog, IMDS, SHA1HULUD runner) on the host and across the fleet; initiate restore-from-backup and org-wide secret rotation.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName =~ "cipher.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/W:")
    or (ProcessCommandLine has "shred" and ProcessCommandLine has "-uvz")
    or (ProcessCommandLine has_all ("del","/F","/Q","/S") and ProcessCommandLine has "USERPROFILE")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (ActingProcessName has "cipher.exe" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "/W:")
    or (ActingProcessCommandLine has "shred" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "-uvz")
    or (ActingProcessCommandLine has_all ("del","/F","/Q","/S") and ActingProcessCommandLine has "USERPROFILE")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CI/dev host exfiltrating to api.github.com shortly after cloud IMDS harvest (Sha1-Hulud exfil chain) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Correlates a package-manager process reaching cloud IMDS with the same host contacting api.github.com/github.com within 30 minutes — the Sha1-Hulud pattern of harvesting cloud secrets then pushing them into a newly created public GitHub repo. This directly targets the 'close the exfiltration gap' thesis of the article: catching secrets leaving CI toward github.com, not after they surface. Rationale: Chains the two documented Sha1-Hulud network behaviours (IMDS credential harvest → push to a new github.com repo) on the same host within a tight window, which is far more specific than either signal alone and maps precisely to the article's exfiltration-to-github concern. Time-window correlation makes it a hunt, not an alert. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/ • https://www.wiz.io/blog/shai-hulud-2-0-ongoing-supply-chain-attack • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/npm-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1567.001 T1552.005
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A Node app on a cloud VM that reads IMDS and also pushes to GitHub (e.g. a release bot / GitOps agent) within the window
  • CI runner that legitimately fetches instance credentials then interacts with the GitHub API for status checks
  • Renovate/Dependabot-style automation touching both IMDS and github.com
  • Container build that queries metadata for a token and pushes an image manifest referencing github.com
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("install","preinstall","postinstall") or RemoteUrl has "api.github.com"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Inspect the github.com interaction — was a NEW repo created (check GitHub audit log for repo.create with an 18-char hex name or description 'Sha1-Hulud: The Second Coming.')? Confirm the IMDS call was install-time. Step 2 (contain): Delete the attacker repo, revoke the developer's GitHub token and the instance role credentials, and isolate the host/runner. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep for bun payload files, trufflehog, and the SHA1HULUD runner on the host; enumerate all public repos org-wide matching the campaign description and rotate every exposed secret.
let LookbackDays = 30d;
let WindowMinutes = 30m;
let Imds = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where RemoteIP == "169.254.169.254" or RemoteUrl has "metadata.google.internal"
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","bun","bun.exe","npm","yarn","pnpm")
    | project ImdsTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, HarvestProc = InitiatingProcessFileName;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("api.github.com","github.com")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","bun","bun.exe","npm","yarn","pnpm","git","git.exe","curl","curl.exe")
| join kind=inner Imds on DeviceId
| where Timestamp between (ImdsTime .. ImdsTime + WindowMinutes)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, ImdsTime, HarvestProc, DelayMin = datetime_diff('minute', Timestamp, ImdsTime)
| order by Timestamp desc
let LookbackDays = 30d;
let WindowMinutes = 30m;

ASCDeviceEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("api.github.com","github.com")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","bun","bun.exe","npm","yarn","pnpm","git","git.exe","curl","curl.exe")
| join kind=inner Imds on DeviceId

| join({#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/(api\.)?github\.com$/i ContextImageFileName=/(node|bun|npm|yarn|pnpm|git|curl)(\.exe)?$/i}, field=aid, include=[DomainName, ContextImageFileName])

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

    by All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest, All_Traffic.dest_port
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| append
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web
        where Web.dest IN ("bold-dhawan.45-139-104-115.plesk.page", "objective-hopper.45-139-104-115.plesk.page", "carte-avantage.com")
        by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.url, Web.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`]
| append
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS
        where DNS.query IN ("bold-dhawan.45-139-104-115.plesk.page", "objective-hopper.45-139-104-115.plesk.page", "carte-avantage.com")
        by DNS.src, DNS.query, DNS.answer
     | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`]
Critical

Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).

Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] The Gentlemen SystemBC C2 beacon to known operator IPs · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains

Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] The Gentlemen wevtutil clearing of Security/System/Application event logs · [LLM] The Gentlemen pre-encryption Volume Shadow Copy deletion · [LLM] The Gentlemen Go encryptor mass file rename to actor extensions · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
The Gentlemen ransomware scheduled task named gentlemen* AIInstallation High
Hunts creation, modification or execution of a Windows scheduled task whose name matches the string 'gentlemen' (e.g. 'gentlemen_system'), the exact SYSTEM-persistence task The Gentlemen affiliates create to launch their Go encryptor. This is a named-artifact detection unique to this actor. Rationale: Article's Execution recommendation literally instructs 'high-severity SIEM alerts for the creation, deletion or execution of any scheduled task matching the string gentlemen*'; external reporting (ESET, Red Piranha) confirms the concrete task name 'gentlemen_system'. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/killing-me-gently-inside-gentlemens-edr-killer-framework/ • https://redpiranha.net/news/the-gentlemen-ransomware-analysis
ATT&CKT1053.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security team red-team engagement re-using the actor's task name for a purple-team exercise
  • Threat-hunt / detection-validation scripts that create a benign task containing 'gentlemen' to test this very rule
  • A legitimately-named business task coincidentally containing the substring (rare)
  • EDR/AV signature that quarantines and re-creates a task with the family name in a comment field
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("purpleknight.exe","atomicred.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the full task definition (Get-ScheduledTask / task XML) and the binary it launches; hash and detonate the target executable and check for Go-compiled encryptor traits. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, disable/delete the task, and block the referenced binary hash tenant-wide. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep all hosts for the same task name and for the follow-on TTPs — ThrottleBlood.sys driver load, wevtutil log clears, and SystemBC beacons to the known C2 IPs.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where (FileName =~ "schtasks.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "gentlemen")
   or (FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has_all ("ScheduledTask","gentlemen"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID in (4698, 4699, 4702) or (EventID == 4688 and NewProcessName endswith "schtasks.exe")
| where EventData has "gentlemen" or CommandLine has "gentlemen"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, EventID, NewProcessName, CommandLine, EventData
| order by TimeGenerated desc

GentleKiller BYOVD: ThrottleBlood.sys vulnerable driver load (CVE-2025-7771) AIExploitation High
Hunts the load or drop of the renamed vulnerable ThrottleStop driver 'ThrottleBlood.sys' that The Gentlemen abuse via CVE-2025-7771 to gain kernel execution and disable EDR. Targets the specific BYOVD artifact of the GentleKiller framework, not generic driver loads. Rationale: Article's Privilege Escalation section names CVE-2025-7771 (ThrottleStop.sys); ESET and Dark Reading confirm the driver is dropped renamed to ThrottleBlood.sys inside the GentleKiller framework — a high-fidelity named BYOVD artifact. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/killing-me-gently-inside-gentlemens-edr-killer-framework/ • https://www.darkreading.com/vulnerabilities-threats/gentlemen-ransomware-vulnerable-driver-security-gear
ATT&CKT1068 T1562.001 T1543.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine ThrottleStop overclocking utility installed by an enthusiast/OEM on an engineering workstation (would be named ThrottleStop.sys, not ThrottleBlood.sys)
  • Security researcher analysing the BYOVD sample in a sandbox VM
  • Vulnerable-driver blocklist testing (Microsoft recommended-driver-block-rules validation)
  • Backup of a driver file copied during forensic imaging
Suppression filter
| where FileName !~ "ThrottleStop.sys" or FolderPath !has @"\Program Files\TechPowerUp\"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the file name — ThrottleBlood.sys is never legitimate; verify the signing cert and whether the driver was actually loaded (service/registry CurrentControlSet\Services). Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host immediately (kernel-level EDR kill likely in progress), and if the driver loaded assume EDR is blinded — pivot to network/firewall telemetry for scoping. Step 3 (hunt): Look for Allpatch2.exe/All.exe execution, subsequent EDR service stops, and the gentlemen_system task on the same and adjacent hosts.
union
(DeviceImageLoadEvents | where Timestamp > ago(7d) | where FileName in~ ("ThrottleBlood.sys","ThrottleStop.sys") | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Kind="ImageLoad", FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine),
(DeviceFileEvents | where Timestamp > ago(7d) | where FileName in~ ("ThrottleBlood.sys","ThrottleStop.sys") and FolderPath has_any (@"\Windows\", @"\Temp\", @"\AppData\", @"\Drivers\") | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Kind="FileWrite", FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine)
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFileName in~ ("ThrottleBlood.sys","ThrottleStop.sys")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

GentleKiller EDR-killer binaries Allpatch2.exe / All.exe execution AIInstallation High
Hunts execution of the GentleKiller framework's userland EDR/AV termination tools (Allpatch2.exe, All.exe) that The Gentlemen deploy after gaining kernel privileges via the ThrottleBlood BYOVD. Named-binary detection specific to this actor's tooling. Rationale: Article names the 'GentleKiller' EDR-killer framework; Securonix/Red Piranha reporting confirms the concrete deployed binaries Allpatch2.exe and All.exe (plus leaked HexKiller/HavocKiller), making these exact filenames high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://connect.securonix.com/threat-research-intelligence-62/the-gentlemen-raas-and-the-gentlekiller-edr-killer-framework-389 • https://redpiranha.net/news/the-gentlemen-ransomware-analysis
ATT&CKT1562.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A benign internal utility coincidentally named all.exe (build/batch wrapper) — pivot on parent process and folder path
  • Malware analyst executing the sample in a lab
  • Generic 'all.exe' shipped by a niche third-party installer in Program Files
  • Detection-validation tooling renaming a harmless binary to test the rule
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Temp\", @"\AppData\", @"\Users\Public\", @"\Windows\Temp\") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Verify the file hash/path — legitimate all.exe lives in a vendor Program Files dir; GentleKiller variants run from Temp/AppData/user-writable paths. Check whether EDR/AV services stopped immediately after. Step 2 (contain): Isolate host, re-assert EDR tamper protection, block the hashes. Step 3 (hunt): Correlate with the preceding ThrottleBlood.sys load and following file-encryption / VSS deletion on the same host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("Allpatch2.exe","All.exe","HexKiller.exe","HavocKiller.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\Allpatch2.exe","\\All.exe","\\HexKiller.exe","\\HavocKiller.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

The Gentlemen wevtutil clearing of Security/System/Application event logs AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts use of wevtutil (or PowerShell Clear-EventLog / Wevtutil cl) to clear the Security, System and Application logs — the anti-forensic step The Gentlemen use to remove audit trails after EDR kill and before encryption. Rationale: Article's Defense Impairment recommendation calls for 'behavioral alerts for systems executing wevtutil to clear Security/System logs'; Microsoft's write-up confirms the Go encryptor clears System/Application/Security logs via wevtutil. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/05/28/the-gentlemen-ransomware-dissecting-a-self-propagating-go-encryptor/
ATT&CKT1070.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmin manually clearing bloated logs during troubleshooting
  • SCCM/Intune remediation scripts that clear a specific log channel
  • Golden-image / sysprep pipeline clearing logs before capture
  • Log-forwarding agent that clears local logs after shipping
  • Backup software rotating event logs
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("ccmexec.exe","tiworker.exe","omadmclient.exe") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "sysprep"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm which logs were cleared and by which account/parent; a Security-log clear (EID 1102) from a non-admin-workstation context is high signal. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host and preserve any forwarded copies of the cleared logs from the SIEM (they survive local clearing). Step 3 (hunt): Treat as late-stage — immediately sweep for encryption activity, gentlemen_system task, and SystemBC C2 on the host and its segment.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where (FileName =~ "wevtutil.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_any (" cl ","clear-log") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Security","System","Application"))
   or (FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has "Clear-EventLog")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688 and NewProcessName endswith "wevtutil.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any (" cl ","clear-log") and CommandLine has_any ("Security","System","Application")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

The Gentlemen internal reconnaissance via Advanced IP Scanner AIReconnaissance Medium
Hunts execution of Advanced IP Scanner (advanced_ip_scanner.exe), the network mapping tool The Gentlemen affiliates repeatedly use for internal discovery prior to lateral movement and self-propagation. Rationale: Article's Discovery recommendation explicitly says to 'Monitor for internal usage of tools such as Advanced IP Scanner, which the threat actors frequently use for internal network reconnaissance'; corroborated by Securelist/Microsoft campaign reporting. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/the-gentlemen-raas/120447/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/05/28/the-gentlemen-ransomware-dissecting-a-self-propagating-go-encryptor/
ATT&CKT1046 T1018
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT/helpdesk staff legitimately using Advanced IP Scanner for asset inventory
  • MSP tooling that bundles the scanner
  • Network engineer troubleshooting connectivity
  • Vulnerability-assessment engagement
  • Portable copy run by a curious power user
Suppression filter
| where AccountName !in~ ("svc_netops","helpdesk_admin") and FolderPath has_any (@"\Temp\", @"\Downloads\", @"\AppData\", @"\Users\Public\")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Determine whether the executing account is an IT/network role and whether the host normally runs scanning tools; check the folder path (Temp/Downloads/AppData is suspicious). Step 2 (contain): If unsanctioned, isolate host and review outbound SMB/RDP fan-out that follows the scan. Step 3 (hunt): Look for subsequent SMB self-propagation (CVE-2025-33073), Advanced IP Scanner output files, and credential access on discovered hosts.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName =~ "advanced_ip_scanner.exe" or ProcessVersionInfoProductName has "Advanced IP Scanner" or ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName =~ "advanced_ip_scanner.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "advanced_ip_scanner.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

The Gentlemen SystemBC C2 beacon to known operator IPs AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts outbound network connections to the confirmed SystemBC SOCKS5 C2 servers used by The Gentlemen affiliates (193.233.202.17, 77.110.122.137, 45.86.230.112), including the observed beacon port 44729. Anchored on validated infrastructure IOCs. Rationale: Article's C2 recommendation calls to 'monitor for anomalous outbound traffic... matching known SystemBC communication signatures'; the three C2 IPs are validated by Huntress/Check Point/Securelist (193.233.202.17 on port 44729, 45.86.230.112 SOCKS5), meeting the second-source confirmation bar. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/the-gentlemen-raas/120447/ • https://redpiranha.net/news/the-gentlemen-ransomware-analysis
ATT&CKT1090 T1071.001 T1219
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel platform or sandbox in the environment actively connecting to the IOC IPs for enrichment/detonation
  • Security scanner probing the IP range
  • IP re-assigned to a benign hoster after takedown (validate against current TI freshness)
  • Honeypot / deception host deliberately reaching the C2
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe") and DeviceName !has "sandbox"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the initiating process and host; a non-browser process (svchost, rundll32, or the Go encryptor) beaconing to these IPs is confirmation. Step 2 (contain): Block the three IPs at the firewall/proxy, isolate the beaconing host, and capture the SystemBC binary for hashing. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the initiating process hash across the fleet, and sweep for GentleKiller/ThrottleBlood and the gentlemen_system task on any host that touched these IPs.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("193.233.202.17","77.110.122.137","45.86.230.112")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, LocalIP
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP in ("193.233.202.17","77.110.122.137","45.86.230.112")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, SourceHostName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, ApplicationProtocol, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

The Gentlemen pre-encryption Volume Shadow Copy deletion AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts deletion of Volume Shadow Copies via vssadmin, wmic shadowcopy, or PowerShell WMI — the backup-inhibition step The Gentlemen perform immediately before file encryption to prevent recovery. Rationale: Article's Impact recommendation calls for 'behavioral alerts for systems using vssadmin and wmic to delete Volume Shadow Copies'; this is the canonical pre-encryption step and legitimate use in user space is rare. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/05/28/the-gentlemen-ransomware-dissecting-a-self-propagating-go-encryptor/
ATT&CKT1490
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Veeam/commvault backup pre-snapshot cleanup
  • Sysadmin VSS storage troubleshooting (vssadmin resize/delete)
  • Windows Server backup lifecycle removing old snapshots
  • SQL/Exchange VSS-writer maintenance scripts
  • Disk-imaging tool clearing snapshots pre-capture
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("veeam.backup.shell.exe","vssvc.exe","wbengine.exe","cveagent.exe") and InitiatingProcessParentFileName !=~ "services.exe"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify parent process and account — a service account or the Go encryptor deleting shadows is far more suspicious than backup software. Check for concurrent mass file writes. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host immediately (encryption imminent/underway) and preserve any offsite/immutable backups. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep the segment for the encrypted-extension file writes, wevtutil clears, and SystemBC beacons — deletion is typically the final pre-lock step.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where (FileName =~ "vssadmin.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "delete shadows")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_all ("shadowcopy","delete"))
   or (FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Win32_Shadowcopy","Remove-WmiObject Win32_Shadowcopy"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where (NewProcessName endswith "vssadmin.exe" and CommandLine has "delete shadows")
   or (NewProcessName endswith "wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "shadowcopy" and CommandLine has "delete")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: The Gentlemen Volume Shadow Copy Deletion
id: 9a4d2c81-3e76-4b58-a1f9-2d6b8e3c5f11
description: Detects Volume Shadow Copy deletion via vssadmin/wmic/PowerShell as performed by The Gentlemen ransomware before encryption.
references:

level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 ((@Image:(*\vssadmin.exe OR *\VSSADMIN.EXE) AND @CommandLine:*"delete shadows"*) OR (@Image:(*\wmic.exe OR *\WMIC.EXE) AND @CommandLine:(*shadowcopy* AND *delete*)))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ((ImageFileName=/vssadmin\.exe$/i CommandLine=/delete\s+shadows/i) OR (ImageFileName=/wmic\.exe$/i CommandLine=/shadowcopy/i CommandLine=/delete/i)) | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name=vssadmin.exe AND Processes.process="*delete shadows*") OR (Processes.process_name=wmic.exe AND Processes.process="*shadowcopy*" AND Processes.process="*delete*") OR (Processes.process_name IN (powershell.exe,pwsh.exe) AND Processes.process="*Win32_Shadowcopy*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
The Gentlemen Go encryptor mass file rename to actor extensions AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts high-volume file creation/rename to The Gentlemen's known encrypted-file extensions (.7mtzhh, .ojuopo, .umc16h) by a single process — the encryption impact stage of the self-propagating Go encryptor. Rationale: Second-source reporting (Red Piranha, ESET) confirms The Gentlemen append distinct extensions .7mtzhh, .ojuopo and .umc16h to encrypted files; bursts of a novel high-entropy extension from one process is a low-FP impact signal. Cross-checked against: • https://redpiranha.net/news/the-gentlemen-ransomware-analysis • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/killing-me-gently-inside-gentlemens-edr-killer-framework/
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A backup/archival tool that appends a random-looking suffix (rare, and usually consistent per vendor)
  • Detection-validation run using a benign renamer against test files
  • A developer build artifact pipeline generating many files with an unusual extension (would differ from these exact strings)
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the initiating process hash and whether files are becoming unreadable/high-entropy; identify the earliest affected host and share. Step 2 (contain): Isolate all affected hosts, kill the encryptor process, and revoke the service account it runs under; protect immutable backups. Step 3 (hunt): Trace back to the gentlemen_system task, ThrottleBlood/GentleKiller activity, and SystemBC C2 to scope the full intrusion and the SMB self-propagation path.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileModified")
| where FileName endswith ".7mtzhh" or FileName endswith ".ojuopo" or FileName endswith ".umc16h"
| summarize FileCount = count(), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), Sample = any(FolderPath) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessSHA256, bin(Timestamp, 5m)
| where FileCount > 50  // 50 = mass-encryption threshold; a legit rename batch rarely hits a novel 6-8 char extension
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileModified")
| where TargetFileName endswith ".7mtzhh" or TargetFileName endswith ".ojuopo" or TargetFileName endswith ".umc16h"
| summarize FileCount = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), Sample = any(TargetFilePath) by DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where FileCount > 50  // mass-encryption burst threshold
| order by FirstSeen desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @TargetFilename:(*.7mtzhh OR *.ojuopo OR *.umc16h)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/\.(7mtzhh|ojuopo|umc16h)$/i | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName], function=count()) | count > 50
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count values(Filesystem.file_path) as paths from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name="*.7mtzhh" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.ojuopo" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.umc16h") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user _time span=5m | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | where count > 50 | sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count values(Filesystem.file_path) as paths from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name="*.7mtzhh" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.ojuopo" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.umc16h") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user _time span=5m | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | where count > 50 | sort - count
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
